Commentators pair the ayah consistently with passages saying even the Prophet could not guide whom he loved, so the limit applies to everyone rather than marking anyone's failure.

crossReferences.why: States that even the Prophet cannot guide whom he loves, and that God guides whom He wills.
Uses the same rare verb of reversal a few ayat later, of a closely related group.
Says guiding them is not upon you, in the middle of an instruction about giving.

studies.applyIt: Think of a person you have been trying to change, and count how many conversations you have spent on it. Then decide what you will still do for them once you stop trying. This ayah sets a limit on one kind of effort, and the useful question is what remains available after that limit is accepted.

studies.title: Wishing You Were The Same
studies.meaning: The passage concerns a specific group in a state of open war: people who had professed belief, returned to the opposing side, and went on fighting from there. What is described is a wartime measure against combatants, and it is bounded immediately. The very next ayah removes from it anyone under treaty, anyone unwilling to fight either side, and anyone who withdraws and offers peace. Commentators read the two ayat together as one passage.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the years of open conflict between Medina and Mecca. Commentators describe people who had joined the community and then left it, carrying what they knew and acting against it from outside, and read the passage as addressing that. The reports differ over which group is meant while agreeing on the wartime setting. The exception follows in the next breath.

keyTerms.note: From the same root as the word for affection used earlier in this surah. The wish described is for equivalence, that the difference between the two sides should disappear altogether.
A word for evenness, from the root meaning to make something level. The wish is not for conversion but for sameness, which would remove any ground for the community to stand apart.
The plural of the word for a close ally, used throughout this surah. In that society an alliance carried military obligation, so the term names a formal commitment rather than a friendship.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliance in Arabia was a declared and binding arrangement: it committed a group to fight alongside another and to shelter them. Switching sides during a conflict was a recognised danger, since a party that had lived among you knew your defences and your numbers. The passage addresses that hazard in a setting where no neutral authority existed to adjudicate.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction in this ayah is qualified twice over in the ayah immediately following, which names three separate categories it does not touch: those linked by treaty, those unwilling to fight either side, and those who withdraw and offer peace. The classical commentaries treat the two ayat as a single unit for that reason.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage belongs to the Quran's treatment of one specific armed conflict, and its shape is instructive. A measure is stated and then bounded in the next breath, with the boundaries drawn around anyone who steps back from fighting. That structure recurs across the Quran's passages on war, where the withdrawal of hostility consistently removes the ground for any response.

crossReferences.why: Immediately removes several categories from this, including anyone who withdraws and offers peace.
Instructs the community to incline to peace if the other side inclines to it, relying on God.
Sets a limit on fighting and warns against transgressing it in any circumstance whatever.

studies.applyIt: Read this ayah together with the one after it, which is how the commentaries handle it, and notice what the second takes away from the first. Passages like this get quoted alone far more often than they are read in place. Getting into the habit of reading the next ayah is a small discipline with a large effect.

studies.title: No Way Against Them
studies.meaning: A series of exceptions is set out, and each narrows what came before. Those connected to a people bound by treaty are excluded. So are those who arrive with their chests constricted at the thought of fighting either side. Then a general clause covers anyone who withdraws, does not fight, and offers peace, and the ayah says God has left no way against them. Commentators treat that final clause as decisive.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly on a wartime instruction and limiting it. Commentators describe a situation in which some tribes were tied to Medina by treaty while others were caught between commitments they could not reconcile. The exceptions named correspond to real groups in that landscape rather than to hypothetical cases, which is how the classical commentaries read them.

keyTerms.note: A physical description of reluctance, the tightness felt facing something one cannot do. It names an inner condition as grounds for exemption, which is unusual in a passage of this kind.
From a root meaning to separate oneself and stand apart. It describes a deliberate stepping back rather than a defeat, and that stepping back is what the exception is built on.
From the root that gives peace, safety and greeting. The phrase used is literally to cast peace toward someone, which pictures an offer thrown across a distance between parties.

keyTerms.gloss: a way, a course of action
keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for a road. Saying God has made no way for you against them closes off the possibility entirely rather than merely discouraging anyone from pursuing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tribal life produced men with obligations on both sides of a conflict: a mother's people here, a father's there, a treaty binding one and blood binding the other. Such men often tried to stay out of a war entirely and were distrusted by everyone for it. This ayah's second exception describes exactly that person, and protects him.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah names the constriction of a person's chest as grounds for exemption, so an inner state is given real weight in a passage about conflict. Commentators note the unusual move: the exception rests not on a treaty or a declaration but on a reluctance only the person feeling it could report.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage narrows a wartime instruction three separate times, and its final clause frames that narrowing as something God has done rather than a concession granted. That matters: the absence of any way against a peaceful party is presented as a fact about the moral landscape, not as leniency chosen by the stronger side. Peace offered is enough to close the matter.

crossReferences.why: States the instruction this ayah immediately limits, and is read together with it throughout.
Instructs inclining toward peace whenever the other side inclines toward it as well.
Warns against denying the sincerity of someone who offers peace, out of desire for gain.

studies.applyIt: Think of a disagreement where the other person has already stepped back and you have not. Perhaps they stopped replying, or conceded, or simply went quiet. Notice whether you are still building the case. This ayah closes a matter the moment the other side withdraws, and most private conflicts end long before we agree to stop.

studies.title: Security From Both Sides
studies.meaning: A third group is described, distinct from the two before it. They want safety from the community and safety from their own people, and whenever they are pulled back toward the conflict they plunge into it. The passage then states the conditions under which they are treated as combatants, and every condition is a failure to do something: not withdrawing, not offering peace, not restraining their hands. All three exits stay open.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing a sequence about groups positioned between two sides in an active war. Commentators identify the people described as tribes who approached Medina seeking safety while continuing to join the other side when pressed. The reports vary over identification and agree on the pattern. The passage belongs to a specific conflict and is read by the tradition in that setting.

keyTerms.note: From a verb for testing metal in fire. It covers persecution, temptation and internal conflict together, and commentators read it here as the surrounding war they kept being pulled into.
A passive form of the rare verb for overturning used a few ayat earlier of a different group. The passive suggests being carried rather than choosing, without excusing the outcome.
The same phrase used earlier in this surah of the instruction given during the Meccan years. Its reuse makes restraint the standard being applied to both parties alike.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A small tribe caught between two larger powers had a genuinely impossible position, and playing both sides was a recognised survival strategy rather than some peculiar vice. It was also understood by everyone as exactly what it was. The problem this ayah addresses is not moral confusion but a party that returned to fighting each time pressure rose.
studies.didYouKnow: The three conditions named in this ayah are all stated negatively, as things not done: not withdrawing, not offering peace, not restraining their hands. Commentators note that the construction leaves three separate exits open, since meeting any one of them would place a person outside what the ayah describes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage concerns a divided interior expressed in repeated action. What it describes is not exactly deception but an inability to hold a position under pressure, recorded without pretending to be anything else. Its conditions then measure conduct rather than sincerity, since conduct is the only thing the other party is actually able to observe.

crossReferences.why: Names the categories placed outside this, including anyone who withdraws and offers peace.
Uses the same rare verb of reversal a few ayat earlier, of a related group in the city.
Sets limits on fighting and warns against transgressing them in any circumstance at all.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you are keeping yourself safe with two groups at once by saying different things in each. Everyone does some version of this, and it rarely feels like dishonesty from the inside. Pick the smaller of the two positions and say it in the other room this week, then see what actually happens.

studies.title: Unless By Mistake
studies.meaning: The passage opens by saying this should never happen at all, and then addresses the case where it happens by accident. Three situations are distinguished by the standing of the person killed, and each carries its own combination of a freeing and a compensation paid to the family, which the family may waive. Where the means are absent, a period of fasting stands in place of them, and the whole is named a turning toward God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators report a case in which a man was killed by mistake during a period of conflict, when a person's affiliation was not always visible, and read the passage as addressing that kind of situation. The reports differ over the incident and agree on the setting. The surah is dealing here with the practical consequences of a war fought between people who knew each other.

keyTerms.note: From a root for missing a mark, the opposite of hitting it. The word describes an act that went astray rather than one intended, which is the entire basis of the distinction drawn.
A payment made to the relatives of someone killed, an institution that long predated the Quran in Arabia. Its retention here sets a familiar practice inside a new framework of accountability.
Literally the freeing of a neck. The Quran repeatedly attaches this to expiation, so that a wrong done is answered by removing someone else's bondage and not by payment alone.
The word for returning to God. Applying it to the whole set of measures makes them a movement of the person responsible rather than the settlement of an outstanding debt.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Killing in Arabia set off obligations that could run for generations. A family that lost a man could demand blood or accept payment, and which they chose shaped relations between tribes for decades. Compensation existed precisely because feuds were ruinous, and everyone understood the arithmetic. This passage works inside that system rather than replacing it wholesale.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage distinguishes three cases by the standing of the person killed, and in one of them, a believer among a hostile people, no compensation goes to the family and only a freeing is asked. Commentators explain that paying compensation there would have strengthened the opposing side during an active conflict.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An accident is treated as carrying real weight without being treated as a crime, which is a difficult balance to hold. Something must be done, and what is asked has three components: a person freed, a family compensated, and a turning toward God. That last element keeps the whole from being a transaction, since the person responsible is understood to have been changed.

crossReferences.why: States the entirely different case of deliberate killing, in the ayah immediately after this.
Says the taking of one life without cause is like the killing of all humanity together.
Addresses the family's option to forgo retaliation, and calls that a lightening and a mercy.

studies.applyIt: Think of harm you caused without meaning to and settled by apologising. This passage asks for something beyond the apology: an actual act, costly enough to be felt. Choose one and do it quietly, without telling the person concerned. The point is not to reopen anything but to let the thing register somewhere.

studies.title: Deliberately, And What Follows
studies.meaning: The other case, stated in one sentence and answered with four consequences stacked on each other: the Fire, permanence, God's anger, and a cutting off, followed by a great punishment. Commentators note that nothing else in the Quran attracts this precise accumulation. They also discuss at length whether the permanence is absolute or emphatic, and record a genuine range of positions rather than one settled answer.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after the passage on accidental killing, and read against a background in which blood feuds and revenge killings were an ordinary feature of Arabian life. Commentators report that the severity of the ayah was itself remarked upon by the early community. No single occasion is reported, and it is read as a general statement rather than a response to one incident.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning a pillar or a support, so the verb suggests leaning on something on purpose. Intent is described as something a person props themselves against rather than merely has.
A word for a return matched to what was given. Its use makes the punishment described a correspondence rather than an addition, which is how the Quran generally frames consequence.
The verb for anger, used of God sparingly across the Quran. Commentators discuss what it means when applied to God and generally read it as naming a relation of rejection.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Revenge killing was embedded in Arabian life and was often thought honourable. A man who did not avenge a relative lost standing, and killing inside a feud carried no shame at all. Against that background, an ayah attaching this weight to deliberate killing addressed something its audience had not previously understood as a matter of ultimate consequence.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where four consequences are stacked in a single sentence in quite this way. Commentators through the classical period discussed at length whether the permanence stated here is absolute or an intensification, and the tradition preserves several positions rather than resolving into one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Deliberate killing is placed at the extreme of what the Quran describes, and the classical discussion around the ayah is itself significant: scholars held its severity together with the wide promise of forgiveness stated earlier in this same surah, and declined to collapse either into the other. That tension is preserved in the tradition rather than resolved away.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the accidental case just before, with a completely different set of consequences.
States earlier in this surah that God forgives anything short of associating partners with Him.
Names killing among the gravest wrongs, then describes repentance and a changing of deeds.

studies.applyIt: Sit with how far this ayah goes, and notice that the tradition never smoothed it out. Then consider the smaller cruelties you allow yourself, the ones that damage a person slowly rather than at once. The distance between the two is real, and it is also shorter than most of us prefer to think.

studies.title: You Were Like This Before
studies.meaning: A single instruction, given twice for emphasis: establish the facts. The specific error named is telling someone who offers you a greeting of peace that his belief is not genuine, and the motive named is gain. Then comes the sentence that changes the register entirely. You were like this once, and God favoured you. The argument against the error is not a rule but a memory the hearer has to supply.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators report an incident during an expedition in which a man who greeted a party with a declaration of peace was killed and his possessions taken, on the assumption that he was declaring it only to save himself. The reports differ over names and details while agreeing on the substance, and describe this ayah as the response to what happened.

keyTerms.note: From the root for separation and distinction, so the verb means making a thing clear by setting it apart. It appears twice in this ayah, opening the instruction and then closing it.
A word for something that passes across, used of temporary things. Naming the motive with this word evaluates it in the same breath as identifying what the motive actually was.
The word for peace, used here of the greeting itself. The person is killed for the very act by which he declared he was not an enemy, which is what the ayah exposes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A traveller meeting an armed party in open country had one instrument available: a greeting, called out loudly enough to be heard at a distance. It was the recognised signal that one came without hostility. Treating that greeting as a trick removed the only protection an unarmed man had, which is why this ayah addresses the greeting directly.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to verify appears twice inside a single ayah, opening and closing the same sentence. Commentators note the repetition as unusual even for a book that repeats often, and read it as bracketing the whole argument, so that everything between the two occurrences sits inside one insistence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument is made through memory rather than through principle. You were once in the position of the person standing in front of you, indistinguishable from outside, and something was given to you that you had not earned. That places the failure in forgetting rather than in ignorance, and makes gratitude for one's own history the ground on which another person's claim is heard.

crossReferences.why: Instructs verification of a report before acting, so that no people are harmed in ignorance.
Removes any course of action against those who withdraw from fighting and offer peace.
Reminds the community that they were once few and weak, before God gave them shelter.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose sincerity you doubt, and try to recall a time when yours would have looked equally thin from outside. Most of us have been at that stage and forgotten it quickly. The argument here runs entirely through that memory, and it only works if you actually go and retrieve it.

studies.title: Not Equal, But Both Promised
studies.meaning: A distinction is drawn and then softened twice. Those who stay behind and those who strive with wealth and person are not equal, and one degree separates them. Then a clause arrives mid-sentence: except those with a genuine impediment, who are removed from the comparison altogether. And then the wider statement that God has promised good to both. Commentators note that the passage ranks without excluding anyone from the promise.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the years of conflict. Commentators report that the clause concerning impediment was added after a man who could not see asked whether the first part of the ayah applied to him. The reports agree on the substance of that incident. The passage stands at the close of the surah's long section on those who went and those who stayed.

keyTerms.note: A participle from the verb to sit. It describes a position rather than delivering a judgement, which is why the ayah can go on to promise good to these people as well.
A word for damage or injury, used here of a condition that prevents someone from acting. It covers limitation broadly rather than naming any particular kind of disability.
From the root for a stair or a rank. A single step is named, which measures the difference precisely rather than describing an unbridgeable gap between the two groups.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A community mobilising left behind the old, the ill, those with no mount and those needed at home, and the difference between going and staying was intensely visible. Those who remained watched the others leave and lived afterwards with what that had looked like. An ayah that both ranked and reassured was addressing a real wound inside a small settlement.
studies.didYouKnow: Commentators report that the clause exempting those with an impediment was added to this ayah after a man who could not see raised the question. Whatever one makes of every detail in the reports, the tradition preserves that sequence, and the clause sits in the ayah as an interruption of an otherwise continuous sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage manages to rank without condemning, which is unusual. One degree separates two groups, and the same sentence promises good to both, so the ranking never becomes an exclusion. The exemption then removes capacity from the comparison entirely, which means what is actually being measured is what a person did with what they had available.

crossReferences.why: States that no blame lies on the blind, the lame or the ill, in a closely similar exemption.
Says there is no way against the weak or ill who are sincere toward God and His Messenger.
States that God burdens no soul beyond its capacity, the principle underlying such exemptions.

studies.applyIt: Compare yourself to someone this week, then correct the comparison for what each of you actually had available: time, health, money, a family that helped or did not. This ayah makes that correction explicitly, in a clause inserted mid-sentence, and the corrected comparison is usually both fairer and more useful.

studies.title: Degrees, Forgiveness And Mercy
studies.meaning: A three-item list completing the sentence before it, and the sequence matters. Ranks are named first, then forgiveness, then mercy, so what began as a comparison of effort ends in something not earned at all. Commentators note that the plural for degrees is left indefinite, so neither their number nor their distance is stated. The closing divine names repeat the last two items, turning the list into a description of God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the second half of a statement about those who strove and those who remained behind. The ayah is short because it completes a longer sentence rather than beginning one, and commentators treat the two as a single unit. It closes the surah's extended section on the community's conduct during conflict, before the passage turns to migration.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a stair, left indefinite here. The preceding ayah named one degree; this one opens into an unspecified number, which commentators read as a deliberate widening.
From a root meaning to cover something protectively, as a helmet covers the head. Forgiveness in Arabic is pictured as the concealment of a fault rather than as its erasure.
From the root that also gives the word for a womb. The connection is old and deliberate, tying mercy to the relation between a mother and what she carries.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rank in Arabian society was public and finely graded: where you sat in a gathering, whose name came first in a recitation of lineage, who spoke before whom. Everyone knew their place in that order and could name the people above and below them. A promise of degrees was therefore heard by a society that already measured itself in those terms.
studies.didYouKnow: The two divine names closing this ayah, the Forgiving and the Merciful, appear together at the end of ayat more often than any other pairing in the Quran. Their placement here repeats, as names, the two things the ayah has just promised, so promise and promiser share one vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sequence does something specific. Ranks imply measurement and comparison, and the two words that follow undercut exactly that: forgiveness addresses what falls short, and mercy is not earned at all. So the ayah ends its account of striving by naming two things that no amount of striving produces, which keeps the ranking from becoming a ledger.

crossReferences.why: Draws the distinction this ayah completes, between those who strove and those who remained.
States that all have degrees according to what they did, and God is not unaware.
Says God raises in degrees those who believe and those given knowledge among you.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this short ayah moves from ranking to forgiveness in three words. Whatever you are currently measuring yourself against, put beside it one thing you were simply given and did not earn. Hold both. The passage does not choose between them, and the discomfort of holding both is roughly the point.

studies.title: Was God's Earth Not Vast
studies.meaning: A conversation at the moment of death, reported as dialogue. The angels ask what condition these people were in; the answer given is that they were kept powerless and could not act; and the reply is a question about the size of the earth. Commentators are careful to read this against the following ayah, which exempts those who genuinely had no means. What is being addressed is the excuse rather than the difficulty.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators identify those described as people who had accepted the message in Mecca and stayed, and in some reports went out with the opposing side. The reports differ over which individuals are meant while agreeing that the passage concerns those who could have left and did not. The exemption in the next ayah is treated as part of the same statement.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to receive something completely, used of collecting a debt in full. Death is described as the taking of what is owed rather than as an ending or a loss.
A passive form, so the weakness is inflicted rather than owned. The same word is used a few ayat earlier of people the community was being urged to act for.
An adjective for wide open space, from a root meaning to have room. Applied to God's earth it answers a claim of confinement by describing the size of what was available.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving Mecca meant abandoning a house, a share in a family business, and the protection of a clan, in order to arrive somewhere as a dependent. It was neither romantic nor easy, and some who could have gone chose the security they had. Everyone in Medina knew both kinds of people, and knew which relatives had made which choice.
studies.didYouKnow: The exchange here is one of very few places in the Quran that report a conversation at the moment of death as direct speech from both sides. Commentators note that the questions asked are open ones, so the excuse is spoken by the person themselves rather than summarised by the narrator.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An excuse is treated as something answerable, which implies excuses are examined rather than simply accepted or dismissed. The reply is a question about available options, and the next ayah exempts precisely those for whom no option existed. Taken together the two establish that responsibility is proportioned to capacity, and that a claim of having no capacity is itself checked.

crossReferences.why: Exempts those who genuinely had no means and no way out, and holds out pardon for them.
Tells those mindful of God that His earth is spacious, using the same argument about room.
Addresses believing servants directly: My earth is wide, so worship Me within it.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you have described to yourself as impossible and write down what you would actually have to give up in order to do it. Not to shame yourself into it. Some things really are impossible, and the next ayah says so plainly. But writing it down is what separates the two cases.

studies.title: No Means And No Way
studies.meaning: An exception is stated and then answered with mercy. Those named are men, women and children who could contrive nothing and could find no route out, and the two clauses cover different lacks: the absence of means, and the absence of any knowledge of where to go. What follows is expressed with a particle of possibility rather than a promise, which the commentators discuss, generally reading it as certainty phrased with restraint.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately qualifying the preceding ayah. Commentators report that some believers in Mecca were genuinely unable to leave, lacking money, an escort, or permission from those who held them, and that this passage concerns them. The reports name individuals in some accounts and describe the category in others, agreeing throughout on the substance of the exemption.

keyTerms.gloss: a means, a way of contriving
keyTerms.note: A word for a device or stratagem, from a root about turning something around. It names practical capacity, the ability to arrange something, rather than willingness or courage.

keyTerms.gloss: find a way, know the route
keyTerms.note: The verb for being guided, applied to a road. It names a second and different lack: not only no means but no knowledge of where the road actually runs.
An intensive form from a root meaning to erase a trace, as wind erases footprints in sand. It suggests removal of the mark rather than merely the withholding of punishment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A journey from Mecca to Medina crossed several days of desert and required a mount, provisions, and someone who knew the wells. A person without money or standing could not simply set out, and a woman or a child could not travel unaccompanied at all. The two conditions named here describe exactly what such a journey required.
studies.didYouKnow: The particle of possibility used here also opens statements about God's forgiveness elsewhere in the Quran. Commentators note that when the word appears with God as its subject, the tradition reads it as certainty expressed in the form of hope, since nothing conditions God and the restraint belongs to the address.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exemption is granted for incapacity rather than for intention, which is precise: nothing is said about what these people felt or wanted. What matters is that no route existed. That places moral responsibility strictly inside the range of the possible, and the pardon offered afterwards is stated in a divine name rather than as a decision, making it a matter of character.

crossReferences.why: Presses the excuse that this ayah exempts, and the two are read together as one statement.
States that God burdens no soul beyond its capacity, the principle behind this exemption.
Describes people in exactly this condition, calling out for a protector and a helper.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you have quietly judged for not getting out of a situation: a job, a marriage, a country, a debt. List what leaving would actually require of them, item by item. This exemption turns on means and on knowing a route, and most judgements of that kind collapse once the list is written.

studies.title: Room Enough On Earth
studies.meaning: A promise attached to leaving, and it names two things: a place of refuge and space. The first word is unusual, built from a root about forcing an opponent's nose into the dust, so what is promised carries a note of vindication rather than shelter alone. The second half then addresses the person who sets out and dies on the road, and states that the recompense has already fallen due upon God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing the passage on those who stayed and those who left. Commentators report that a man who set out from Mecca and died before reaching Medina was the occasion for the second half, and that this ayah settled the question of his standing. The reports differ over his name while agreeing on the incident, which the tradition treats as well established.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning the nose in the dust. Commentators read it as a place where one escapes those who forced the departure, so it carries both shelter and the reversal of humiliation.
From the root for width, used of room and of ample provision together. It answers the fear behind staying, which was that leaving would mean arriving with nothing at all.
A verb for something falling into place, used of a payment becoming due. The recompense is described as settled at the moment of setting out, before there is any arrival.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Emigrants arrived in Medina with nothing and were housed by local families who shared what they had. Some never recovered their former standing; others prospered within a few years. Both outcomes were visible in the city, so a promise of spaciousness was made to people who could see for themselves how uncertain the result of leaving actually was.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for a place of refuge appears only here in the Quran, and it derives from an image of forcing an opponent's face into the dust. Translators generally render it simply as refuge, which loses the note of vindication that the classical commentaries consistently record in it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The second half makes the reward depend on departure rather than on arrival, which detaches it from outcome entirely. A person who dies on the road has already completed what was asked. That is a claim about how intention and action are assessed, and the commentators link it consistently with other passages where God rewards what was undertaken rather than what was achieved.

crossReferences.why: Presses the question of why they did not emigrate, which this ayah answers with a promise.
Promises good in this world to those who emigrated after being wronged, and more beyond.
Tells believing servants that God's earth is wide, so they may worship Him within it.

studies.applyIt: Think of a change you have not made because you cannot see how it would work out. This ayah attaches the recompense to leaving rather than to arriving. Take the first step of that change this week, the smallest one available, and do it without requiring yourself to know what follows from it.

studies.title: When You Travel The Land
studies.meaning: A concession is given for prayer while travelling, and the wording is careful. It says there is no blame rather than issuing an instruction, and it attaches a condition about fearing harm. Commentators discuss that condition at length, some reading travel alone as sufficient and others tying the concession to the danger named, and they record the range. The ayah names the situation rather than resolving the discussion.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a period when journeys out of the city carried real risk. Commentators report that the community continued shortening prayers on journeys after the danger had passed, that the question was raised about it, and that the answer described the concession as a gift given. The reports agree on the substance while differing over the exact wording.

keyTerms.gloss: travel, strike out in the land
keyTerms.note: The verb literally means to strike. Arabic uses it of setting out on a journey, picturing travel as striking the ground with one's feet across a long distance.
From a root meaning to lean or tilt, the same one that gives the word for a wing. A fault is pictured as a leaning away from straightness rather than as a broken rule.

keyTerms.gloss: harm you, put you to trial
keyTerms.note: From the verb for testing metal in fire. It covers attack, persecution and disruption together, which is why commentators discuss what kind of danger the condition actually names.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A journey out of Medina meant days in open country where a party could be seen from a distance and where stopping made you visible. Travellers moved between wells on a schedule set by their water. Anything that shortened a halt reduced exposure, so a concession of this kind carried an immediate practical meaning for anyone who had made the journey.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah uses a phrase for travel that is literally about striking the ground, and the same construction appears elsewhere in the Quran for journeys undertaken to seek provision. Arabic keeps that physical picture inside its ordinary word for travelling, so setting out and striking are named by a single verb.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is framed as the lifting of blame rather than as an instruction, which is a specific shape. Nothing is required; a weight is removed. That framing recurs across the Quran wherever hardship is being accommodated, and it means the concession is described from the perspective of the person carrying the difficulty rather than of the one issuing rules.

crossReferences.why: Continues into the arrangement of prayer under direct threat, in considerably greater detail.
Uses the same shape of concession for the sick and the traveller during the fast.
States that no hardship has been placed upon this community in matters of religion.

studies.applyIt: Notice how reluctant you are to accept a concession offered to you: the lighter version, the shorter route, the help someone volunteered. Many people find it easier to be strict than to be met halfway. This ayah lifts a weight rather than adding one, and accepting that is its own small discipline.

studies.title: Prayer With Weapons Held
studies.meaning: A detailed arrangement is described for praying while an enemy is near: one party stands with the leader, the other faces outward, and they exchange places. The passage then allows weapons to be set down in rain or illness, and repeats the instruction about precaution immediately afterwards. Commentators note how much of the ayah is practical, and that the prayer itself is never suspended, only reorganised around the danger.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a period when the community expected attack while in the field. Commentators connect the arrangement to specific expeditions and record that it was performed in more than one form, transmitting several accounts of how the exchange between the two groups was managed. They treat the variations as evidence of adaptation rather than as disagreement about the passage.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to go around, the same one behind the word for circling. It names a group defined by its movement within the arrangement rather than by its membership.
The plural of a word for a weapon or an instrument. Its repetition several times in one ayah keeps the practical situation continuously present inside a passage about prayer.
The noun for wariness, treated as something taken up. It appears twice here, at the start of the arrangement and again after the concession, closing on caution rather than relief.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An armed party in open country was most vulnerable when it stopped. Setting weapons aside, kneeling, and turning attention away from the horizon was exactly the moment a watching enemy would choose. Everyone who had travelled with a caravan understood this, which is why the arrangement described here reads as tactics rather than as ceremony.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the longest passage in the Quran devoted to the practical arrangement of a prayer, longer than any passage describing prayer in ordinary conditions. Commentators note the imbalance: the manner of praying is set out in real detail only where circumstances make praying difficult.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage assumes prayer continues under conditions that would suspend almost any other activity, and it arranges the danger around the prayer rather than the prayer around the danger. At the same time it takes the danger entirely seriously, repeating the instruction about weapons and precaution. Neither is allowed to displace the other, and that refusal is the substance of the passage.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately with what happens once security returns, restoring the ordinary form.
Gives a briefer provision for prayer in fear, on foot or mounted, in another surah.
Uses the same word for taking precaution earlier in this surah, in a different setting.

studies.applyIt: Think of the thing you drop first when life gets difficult. For most people it is not the urgent thing but the quiet one that holds everything else together. This passage rearranges the difficulty around the practice rather than the practice around the difficulty. Try that once, with whatever your equivalent is.

studies.title: Standing, Sitting, Lying Down
studies.meaning: Three postures are named, and between them they cover every position a body can occupy, which is the point: remembrance is described as continuous where the prayer is bounded. Then the ordinary form is restored once security returns. The closing clause describes the prayer as fixed at appointed times, using a word from the vocabulary of timekeeping, which commentators read as the source of its regularity.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the arrangement for prayer under threat. The sequence is deliberate: the exceptional form is described, then what happens when the exception ends. Commentators read the ayah as closing the passage rather than opening a new subject, and note that it also states the general principle about appointed times, which is otherwise rarely put so directly.

keyTerms.note: The verb covers both calling to mind and saying aloud, which Arabic does not separate. Remembrance in the Quran is therefore never purely internal, and never merely verbal either.
From a root meaning to come to rest, used of ground that stops shaking and of a heart that stops fearing. It names the return of calm rather than the removal of danger.
A passive participle from the root for time, appearing only here in the Quran. It describes something appointed to specific hours rather than merely regular or frequently repeated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in that world was read from the sky and the ground: the length of a shadow, the position of the sun, the first light on the horizon. There were no clocks, and appointments were made by naming a moment of the day everyone could see. A practice fixed to times was tied to the same signs that governed travel, work and rest.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for something fixed to appointed times occurs only here in the Quran, and modern Arabic took the same root for its everyday words for timing and schedule. A term used once in scripture became the ordinary vocabulary of clocks and calendars.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are set beside each other: something bounded by hours, and something unbounded by posture. Remembrance in every position covers the whole of a life, while prayer is fixed to specific moments within it. Neither replaces the other. The structure suggests that a bounded practice is what makes an unbounded one sustainable, rather than competing with it.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who remember God standing, sitting and on their sides, using the same postures.
Contrasts this with those who remember God only a little when they stand for prayer.
Names the times of prayer by the movement of the sun and the recitation of dawn.

studies.applyIt: Pick one posture you are often in and rarely think in: waiting in a queue, lying awake, sitting in traffic. Attach one short remembrance to it this week, the same words each time. This ayah names postures rather than occasions, which is a practical hint about where remembrance actually fits.

studies.title: They Ache As You Ache
studies.meaning: An instruction not to weaken, followed by an argument built entirely on symmetry with one asymmetry inside it. If you are in pain, so are they, in exactly the same way, and the verb repeats three times in a single clause to make the point audible. Then the difference: you expect from God what they do not. Commentators note that the passage concedes the pain rather than denying it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a period after a costly engagement when the community was exhausted. Commentators connect the ayah to a pursuit undertaken while men were still carrying wounds, and describe the instruction as arriving to a group who had every ordinary reason to stop. The reports agree on the setting while differing over which occasion is intended.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be feeble or thin. It describes strength draining away rather than a decision to stop, which is why the instruction addresses a process rather than a choice.
The ordinary verb for suffering pain, physical or otherwise. It occurs three times within one clause here, applied to both sides, and that is what constructs the symmetry.
A verb combining expectation with hope, used of awaiting something you have reason to anticipate. It names the single asymmetry the ayah offers, and it is not about strength.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: After an engagement both sides withdrew carrying wounded men and made camp within a day's ride of each other. Everyone knew the other side was in the same condition, but exhaustion is felt from the inside and only dimly imagined for anyone else. The argument here addressed a group who could see their own casualties and not their opponents'.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic verb for feeling pain appears three times within a single short clause of this ayah, an unusually dense repetition even for a book that repeats deliberately. Commentators read the density as doing the work of the argument, since the sameness is heard before it is understood.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Endurance is grounded in an accurate assessment of the situation rather than in an appeal to strength. Both sides suffer identically, so suffering is not evidence about who is failing. The only difference named is expectation, which is a claim that hope rather than capacity separates people under identical pressure. Nothing is promised anywhere about the outcome itself.

crossReferences.why: Tells the community not to weaken or grieve, since they are the higher if they believe.
Attaches the same recompense to both possible outcomes, removing results from the reckoning.
Describes those who did not weaken at what befell them, nor lose heart, nor give in.

studies.applyIt: When something is hard, you generally compare your inside to other people's outside. Take one situation where you feel you are struggling more than everybody else, and ask honestly what you can actually see of their condition. Usually the answer is very little, and the correction alone changes how long you can keep going.

studies.title: Judge By What You Are Shown
studies.meaning: A statement of purpose for the revelation, and then a boundary. The Book was sent so that judgement between people follows what God has shown rather than what a party presents. The final clause turns to a specific danger, which is becoming an advocate for those who deceive. Commentators note that the warning concerns advocacy rather than error: the risk named is not misjudging but arguing on the wrong side of a case.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical commentaries connect this passage and the ayat after it to a theft in Medina in which the person responsible tried to divert suspicion onto an innocent neighbour, and in which the community initially took his side. The reports agree on the substance of the incident while differing over details, and treat this passage as the correction.

keyTerms.note: A word covering truth, reality and a rightful claim together. Its breadth means the Book is described as sent with what is real and with what is owed, inside a single phrase.
A causative from the verb to see. Judgement is grounded in something shown rather than deduced, which the commentators discuss carefully in relation to how a judge reasons.
From the root for adversarial argument. It names someone who takes a side and argues it, which is precisely the role the closing clause of this ayah warns against occupying.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dispute in Medina was argued publicly by whoever had standing to speak for a family, and eloquence often decided outcomes as much as evidence did. A well-connected family could produce advocates a poorer person had no way to match. The warning against becoming an advocate addresses a system where that was exactly what the powerful sought.
studies.didYouKnow: These ayat are among the few in the Quran that respond to a specific criminal case in Medina, and they run for several ayat rather than one. Commentators note that the passage corrects the community rather than the accused, which is unusual for a text arising out of a wrongdoing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates two things that feel identical from the inside: judging by what is true, and advocating for someone you are already inclined toward. It also implies the second can corrupt the first without the person noticing, since an advocate believes his own case. Grounding judgement in what God has shown then places the standard outside the person exercising it.

crossReferences.why: Instructs standing firmly for justice even against yourselves, your parents and your relatives.
Continues the warning, against arguing on behalf of those who deceive themselves.
Warns that hatred of a people must not lead you away from being just toward them.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last argument you took part in where you were, in effect, someone's advocate. Ask what you would have concluded if you had heard those same facts about a stranger. This ayah's distinction is between judging and taking a side, and most of us slide from one to the other without ever deciding to.

studies.title: Do Not Argue For Them
studies.meaning: Two short instructions following a correction. The first is to seek forgiveness, placed immediately after the warning, which commentators read as covering the community's readiness to take the wrong side. The second closes off arguing on behalf of those who betray themselves. The phrase is exact: the deception is described as aimed at the deceivers rather than at anyone else, which is where the passage locates the damage done.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the passage that arose from a theft in the city in which suspicion was deflected onto an innocent man. Commentators describe a community that had rallied around one of its own before establishing what had happened. These two ayat address that reflex directly, and the sequence moves from correcting the judgement to correcting the impulse behind it.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb meaning to ask for covering. The request is for a fault to be covered rather than argued away, which is the opposite of what the passage has just warned against.
A reflexive form of the verb for betrayal. The construction makes the deceiver into the person deceived, which locates the injury inside the one committing the act.
An intensive form describing a settled pattern rather than a single act. That intensity is what keeps the statement from covering anyone who has betrayed a trust only once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Family and tribe closed around an accused member almost automatically, and failing to do so was itself a kind of betrayal in the eyes of relatives. Standing back while your own man was investigated cost you standing with everyone who shared your name. That reflex is what these ayat work against, and it was extremely strong.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for betrayal in this passage is used reflexively, so the people described are betraying themselves. The Quran uses this construction for several wrongs, including the phrase about wronging one's own soul, and the grammar consistently places the injury back onto the person who committed the act.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction to seek forgiveness comes before the instruction not to defend the guilty, and the order matters. Correction begins with the person being corrected rather than with the offender. The passage then names habitual treachery as what God does not love, using an intensive form, which distinguishes a settled character from a single failure and leaves room for the second.

crossReferences.why: States the standard this passage applies, judging by what God has shown rather than by loyalty.
Asks who will argue on their behalf when the Day of Resurrection actually comes.
Follows with the promise that whoever does wrong and seeks forgiveness will find God forgiving.

studies.applyIt: Notice the moment you start defending someone before you know what happened, usually because they are yours. That instinct is loyalty and it is not worthless. But hold it for one day before speaking, and use the day to find out. Most of the harm here is done in the first hour, by people acting on a good motive.

studies.title: Hidden From People, Not God
studies.meaning: A contrast drawn in one sentence, with the sharpest part in the middle. They conceal themselves from people and cannot conceal themselves from God, and He is with them while they arrange their words in the night. The verb for that arranging is the same one used earlier in this surah of a different group. The closing name describes God as encompassing what they do, surrounding rather than merely observing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, part of the passage arising from a theft in the city in which suspicion was deflected. Commentators describe the plan being made at night, among people who had counted on the community's willingness to believe them. The ayah's picture of nocturnal arrangement matches those reports, and the same verb has appeared earlier in this surah for a comparable situation.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning to try to become hidden, so effort is built into the verb. Concealment is described as something attempted rather than achieved, which the second half of the clause confirms.
From the word for a house or for passing the night. The verb was used earlier in this surah of a different group, linking the two passages by vocabulary rather than by subject.
From a root meaning to enclose on all sides, used of a wall around a garden. It describes knowledge as containment rather than as observation from some distance away.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Houses in Medina stood close together and had thin walls, and privacy meant waiting until everyone slept. Conversations that could not be held in daylight were held after the last prayer, in a courtyard or an inner room. The image in this ayah is exact: night was when people in that city actually arranged things they did not want overheard.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing God as encompassing comes from the same root as the Arabic for a wall or an enclosure. The image is spatial rather than visual, so the ayah describes knowledge as something a person is inside of, which is a different picture from simply being watched.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies the specific illusion that makes concealment feel effective: the audience one hides from is human, and success with that audience feels like success outright. The correction offered is not a threat but a description of position. If God is with them while they plan, the concealment was never even attempted against the party that mattered.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for planning at night, of a different group earlier in this surah.
Says God is with them wherever they are, present as a fourth to any three conferring.
Names God as knowing the treachery of the eyes and whatever the breasts conceal.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you would adjust if one particular person could see it. Not something shameful necessarily, just something you calibrate for an audience. Ask which audience you are actually working for. This ayah's point is not surveillance. It is that most concealment is aimed at the wrong party entirely.

studies.title: Who Will Argue For Them
studies.meaning: The passage ends by turning the community's own behaviour into a question. Here you are, arguing for them in this life, and then two questions follow: who will argue with God on their behalf on that day, and who will stand as their representative. Neither is answered. Commentators note the shift in scale, since one verb for arguing covers both settings, and that repetition is what makes the comparison land.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the sequence that arose from a theft in the city and the community's readiness to defend the accused. Commentators describe the passage as addressed to those who had spoken up before establishing the facts. This ayah completes the correction by projecting the same behaviour forward, and the reports treat the episode as well established.

keyTerms.note: A construction placing two demonstratives together, an emphatic address that points directly at the hearers. It has the tone of turning to face somebody in the middle of a conversation.
From a root meaning to twist a rope tightly. Argument is pictured as two strands wound against each other, which suits a word used here of contesting somebody's case.
A word for someone appointed to act on another's behalf. It is used of God elsewhere in this surah, and the question asks who else could possibly occupy that role.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Legal standing in Arabia ran through representation. A person without a strong advocate had no practical way to press a claim, and families invested in producing men who could speak well. Asking who will represent someone on the Day of Resurrection took the most familiar structure of justice available and removed it, leaving a person alone.
studies.didYouKnow: The same verb for arguing on someone's behalf appears twice within a few ayat of this passage, once closing it off in this life and once asking who could perform it in the next. Commentators note the repetition as binding the passage together, so that a warning and a question turn on one word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage works by projecting a present behaviour into a setting where it becomes visibly futile. Advocacy is real and effective in this world, which is exactly why people invest in it, and the question exposes what it can and cannot reach. The closing question about representation then removes the last structure a person might rely on, leaving the case standing alone.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction this ayah enforces, against arguing for those who deceive themselves.
Describes a day when no soul avails another and no intercession is accepted from it.
Pictures people arriving alone, with none of the intercessors they had claimed beside them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a favour you have relied on being able to call in: a person who would speak for you, smooth something over, vouch for you. Notice how much of your sense of safety rests on it. The ayah is not saying such people are worthless. It asks what remains when they are not in the room.

studies.title: Whoever Wrongs His Own Soul
studies.meaning: Two conditional sentences with different subjects. The first begins with a wrong done and ends, with no interval, in finding God forgiving. Nothing is placed between the seeking and the finding. The commentators note the verb: the person does not so much receive forgiveness as discover that it was already the case. The second sentence closes off a natural evasion by saying the sin is earned against oneself, so nobody else carries it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following a passage about someone who committed a theft and tried to shift the blame onto an innocent man. The commentators report the case in detail, though accounts of the names and circumstances differ. These two ayat are the general conclusion drawn from it: the door back is open, and moving a wrong onto another person is precisely what the surrounding ayat have just refused.

keyTerms.note: The root means to put something where it does not belong, and it also gives the word for darkness. Wrongdoing is described as misplacement, and the first party damaged is the one who does it.
A verb of discovery rather than of receiving. It suggests the forgiveness was there to be found, and that the seeking is what brings a person to where it already was.
Commercial vocabulary for gain made through effort. Applying it to sin makes wrongdoing something worked for and accumulated, held in an account belonging to whoever did the work.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Guilt in a clan society was rarely private. A theft attached to a whole family, and blood money for a killing was raised across the kin group, so wrongdoing was distributed by default. The pressure to push blame outward onto an outsider or a weaker household was practical rather than merely dishonest. These ayat cut against a settlement that everyone listening understood from the inside.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of divine names at the end of each ayah is doing work. The first closes with forgiving and merciful, the second with knowing and wise, so the sentence that offers pardon and the sentence that assigns responsibility are sealed with different attributes. Matching the closing names to the content is a consistent feature of these Medinan passages.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness is described as available before it is asked for, which changes what asking is. The person is not persuading God but locating something. At the same time the second ayah refuses to let mercy blur responsibility: a wrong stays attached to whoever did it, and cannot be transferred to a scapegoat or absorbed by a group. Openness and accountability are stated in adjacent sentences without any tension.

crossReferences.why: Extends the same offer at its widest, addressing those who have wronged themselves greatly.
States that no bearer of burdens carries the burden of another.
Continues the passage, describing the person who throws his own fault onto someone innocent.

studies.applyIt: Think of a fault you have always narrated with a reason attached, the version where circumstances or another person explain most of it. Try telling it once, silently, without the explanation. The ayah puts nothing between asking and finding, and the thing that usually stands in the way is the account we have practised.

studies.title: Blaming An Innocent Person
studies.meaning: A sequence of two acts is described, and the second is treated as separate from the first. Someone commits a fault, and then throws it at a person who did nothing. The verb for that throwing is physical, used of hurling a stone. What is carried away is named with two words, one for a barefaced falsehood and one for plain wrongdoing, so the deflection counts as its own offence rather than as an aggravation of the first.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage arising from a theft in the city in which the person responsible directed suspicion at a neighbour. Commentators read this ayah as stating the principle behind the whole episode, lifting it clear of the particular case. Its wording is general, with no names and no details, which is how the classical commentaries treat its function.

keyTerms.note: The verb for throwing a stone or a spear. Applied to accusation it makes the act physical, something launched at a person, and the same root gives Arabic its word for slandering.
From a root meaning to be free of something, also used of recovering from illness. Innocence is described as being clear of a thing rather than as a quality a person possesses.
A verb for shouldering a load and bearing it away. It pictures the wrong as weight transferred onto the person's own back at the very moment he tried to move it elsewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a city where a theft was investigated by asking neighbours, an accusation moved fast and left a mark that no later finding could remove. There were no records with which to clear a name. A man wrongly named carried it in how people traded with him, married into his family, and spoke of him for years.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for barefaced falsehood in this ayah appeared earlier in the same surah, describing a husband reclaiming a dowry after a separation. The reuse links two very different situations by one term, which is a pattern here: shared vocabulary marking that two passages concern one underlying failure.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the wrong from its concealment and weighs the concealment on its own. That matters because deflection usually feels like self-protection rather than aggression, and the ayah insists that it is aimed at somebody. The image of shouldering a load also makes the transfer fail, since what was pushed onto another ends up carried by the one who pushed.

crossReferences.why: Opens the passage this ayah closes, warning against advocacy for those who deceive.
Asks why believing men and women did not think well of one another when an accusation circulated.
Says those who injure believing men and women without cause bear slander and clear sin.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you let someone else absorb the consequence of something you did, even partly, even by staying quiet while they were blamed. Go back to it this week, at least in words, with the one person who would need to hear it. This ayah counts the silence and the accusation as one act.

studies.title: Taught What You Did Not Know
studies.meaning: A near miss is described and then set aside. A group had resolved to lead the Prophet astray, and the sentence turns twice: they mislead only themselves, and they cannot harm him at all. Then the reason is given, and it is not vigilance but what was given: the Book, wisdom, and knowledge he did not previously have. Commentators note that protection is described as instruction rather than as a shield.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about the theft in which suspicion was deflected and a community briefly took the wrong side. Commentators read this ayah as addressing that episode directly: an attempt was made to secure a judgement by misrepresentation, and it did not succeed. The reports agree on the setting, which the tradition treats as well attested.

keyTerms.note: A verb for an intention that has formed but not yet acted. It describes the group at the point of decision, which is exactly where the ayah says the grace intervened.
From the root for judgement and restraint, connected with a bridle. Paired with the Book, it names the capacity to apply what was given rather than the content of it.
From a root meaning what is left over and abundant. The word frames what was given as excess rather than as entitlement, and it both opens and closes this ayah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A judge in Arabia had no investigators and no records. He heard the parties, weighed reputations, and decided. A well-prepared case presented by respected men was therefore extremely powerful, and a person with fewer connections could be talked into a corner. Everyone hearing this ayah knew how a united family could steer an outcome.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for grace opens and closes this ayah, framing everything between the two occurrences. Arabic uses this kind of bracketing often, and commentators note it here because the material inside the frame holds both an attempted deception and the gift of knowledge, contained within a single term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Protection is described as knowledge rather than as prevention. What kept the outcome right was not that the attempt collapsed on its own but that the person judging had been taught. That places revelation in a practical role, and implies that misleading someone is possible in principle, which is why the outcome is attributed to what was given rather than to natural insight.

crossReferences.why: States the standard of judgement this ayah says was protected, judging by what God showed.
Says God found him unaware and guided him, another statement of knowledge given.
Says he did not know what the Book or faith were, before it was made a light.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision you got right and quietly credited to your own judgement. Trace it back and find the person, the book or the accident that put the relevant knowledge into your hands. Naming that is not false modesty. It is accuracy, and this ayah models it about the one person who could most easily have claimed otherwise.

studies.title: Except Three Kinds Of Talk
studies.meaning: A general judgement with a narrow exception. Most private conferring has no good in it, and then three things are named that do: urging charity, urging what is recognised as good, and setting things right between people. Commentators note that all three face outward, concerning what happens to somebody else. A condition is then attached to the reward, which is that the person sought God's approval by it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the passage about conversations held out of sight in which a plan was made. The ayah generalises from that episode to private counsel as such, and then rescues the practice by naming its legitimate uses. Commentators observe that this surah has been dealing throughout with what is said where others cannot hear it.

keyTerms.note: A noun for talk held apart from others, from a root about being alone with somebody. It names the setting rather than the content, which is why the exception must specify what is said.
From the root for repair. It names restoring a relationship between people rather than fixing an opinion, and the Quran uses it repeatedly of mending what has broken between parties.
A noun from the verb to be pleased, used of God's satisfaction. It names the intended audience of the act, which is the condition the promised reward depends upon.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A quiet word between two people in a small city carried real power. Marriages were arranged in such conversations, feuds settled, and reputations built or broken. Everyone understood that the important decisions of Medina were made in courtyards rather than in public, which is part of why a judgement on private conferring mattered so much.
studies.didYouKnow: The three exceptions in this ayah widen in scope as they go: giving to one person, doing what is recognised as good, and reconciling parties. Commentators often pair the ayah with a well-known report describing reconciliation between people as ranking above voluntary fasting and prayer in what it accomplishes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A form of speech is evaluated by what it is for rather than by whether it is concealed. Privacy is neutral; the question is whose interest is served inside it. Then a further condition is added, since even the three good uses attract reward only where God's approval was sought, which places motive above outcome even in acts whose outcome is plainly beneficial.

crossReferences.why: Instructs that private conferring be about righteousness and mindfulness rather than about sin.
Describes reconciliation between believers as something a community owes its own members.
Warns against using oaths as an obstacle to doing good and reconciling between people.

studies.applyIt: Take one conversation this week that you would normally have about somebody, and have it with them instead. Or spend the private word you were going to use for complaint on setting something right between two people you know. The ayah does not condemn quiet conversations. It asks what yours are for.

studies.title: The Path Of The Believers
studies.meaning: A condition is stated in two parts, and commentators discuss whether they name one thing or two: breaking with the Messenger after guidance has become clear, and following a path other than the believers'. The consequence uses an unusual reflexive image, in which a person is turned toward what he had already turned toward. Nothing new is imposed; the direction he chose is confirmed and he is left holding it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about the theft and the attempt to deflect blame, after which the person responsible left the community. Commentators connect the ayah to that departure while noting that its wording is general. The mention of the believers' path has been discussed extensively in the tradition as bearing on the standing of collective agreement.

keyTerms.note: From the root for splitting in two, the same one used earlier in this surah of a marriage coming apart. It pictures separation as one thing tearing rather than as two parties disagreeing.
From the root for separating one thing from another. Clarity is a precondition of the whole sentence, so what is described is someone who saw the distinction before crossing it.
The same verb appears twice in the clause, once of God and once of the person. The construction makes the outcome a confirmation of a choice rather than a separate response to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving a community in Arabia was not a private decision. A man who broke with his group lost protection, standing, and the right to be avenged, and had to attach himself somewhere else or live entirely exposed. The word for splitting used here carried all of that weight, which is why the ayah pairs it with following another path.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the path of the believers in this ayah became one of the most discussed clauses in the surah, since the classical tradition took it as bearing on the weight of collective agreement among scholars. A single clause inside a passage about a theft became the foundation of a large later literature.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The consequence described is a confirmation rather than an imposition, which is a distinctive shape. A person is turned toward the direction he already faced. That suggests judgement partly consists in being given what one chose, rather than in something arriving from outside. The condition about clarity then keeps the whole from touching anyone who never saw the distinction.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately with the boundary of forgiveness, restating an ayah from earlier in the surah.
Describes those who turn back on their heels after guidance had become clear to them.
Describes this community as a middle one, appointed as witnesses over other people.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often a consequence you resented turned out to be simply more of what you had chosen. This ayah describes that shape rather than a punishment arriving from elsewhere. Look at one direction you are currently facing and ask honestly whether you would want more of it, since more of it is generally what comes.

studies.title: Strayed Into Far Error
studies.meaning: An ayah repeated from earlier in this surah with one change, and the change carries the point. The first occurrence ended by calling association a great fabrication; this one ends by calling it a straying that has gone a long way. So the same boundary is described first as an act and then as a position, and commentators read the two endings as complementary rather than as alternatives to one another.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the long section that the earlier occurrence opened. Commentators note that a considerable stretch of the surah runs between the two, covering theological argument, conflict, and a case of false accusation, and that the repetition brackets the whole of it. No separate occasion is reported for this second occurrence.

keyTerms.note: The verb for losing one's road in open country. It describes a condition rather than an act, which is exactly what distinguishes this ayah's ending from the earlier one.
An adjective of distance applied to the straying. It measures the error by how far from the road a person now stands, not by the size of the step that took them there.
A clause leaving the forgiveness of everything else under God's will. Commentators stress that it neither promises nor withholds, holding hope and seriousness together in one phrase.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Losing the track in the desert was the most ordinary catastrophe of that world. A person did not usually stray by a dramatic turn but by a small deviation held for too long, until the landmarks no longer matched. Distance from the road, rather than the size of the original error, decided whether anyone could get back.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and one earlier in the same surah are almost identical, differing only in their final clause. Near-verbatim repetition inside a single surah is rare in the Quran, and commentators read the pair as a frame around the material between them rather than as a simple restatement of the point.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Describing one thing first as a fabrication and then as a distance says something about how a wrong orientation works. It begins as something done and becomes somewhere one is, and the second is harder to address than the first. The clause about God's will then holds the position open rather than closing it, since a distance is a description and not a verdict.

crossReferences.why: States the same boundary earlier in this surah, ending on fabrication rather than on distance.
Uses the same phrase for a straying that has gone far, there of a different failure.
Calls associating partners with God a great wrong, inside a father's counsel to his son.

studies.applyIt: Think about the small deviations rather than the dramatic ones. Nobody sets out to end up far from where they meant to be. Pick one habit you have been holding at a slight angle for a long time, and correct it slightly this week. Distance accumulates from angles, which is the picture this ayah uses.

studies.title: A Share Of Your Servants
studies.meaning: Two ayat describing what is actually being invoked when God is not. The first names female figures, which commentators explain by the goddesses of the region and the feminine names given to certain objects of veneration, and then reframes the whole practice as invoking something else entirely. The second quotes a claim: a fixed portion of God's servants, stated in the same word the surah used of inheritance shares.
