studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the boundary drawn around forgiveness and turning to what stands on the other side of it. Commentators explain the reference to female figures by the names of deities venerated in Mecca and the surrounding region before the community's founding. The passage then moves from that specific practice to a general account of how such devotion is produced.

keyTerms.note: The plural for female beings. Commentators explain it by the feminine names of pre-Islamic deities and by the objects venerated alongside them, and they record more than one reading of the word.
From a root meaning smooth or bare, used of a tree stripped of its leaves. It suggests something rendered down to pure defiance, with nothing else remaining on it.
The exact phrase this surah used of inheritance shares. Its reuse is pointed, since a claim upon people is being stated in the language of a legal entitlement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shrines across the region held named deities, several of them female, with their own attendants, offerings and pilgrimages. Families had inherited relationships with particular shrines going back generations. Devotion there was neither exotic nor marginal; it was the ordinary religious furniture of the society, which is what makes the reframing in this passage so sharp.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for an apportioned share in this passage is the same one used earlier in the surah for the fixed portions of an inheritance. Putting a claim on people into the vocabulary of legal entitlement is a deliberate echo, and one of several places where this surah reuses its own terms across very different subjects.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage relocates the object of devotion without disputing the sincerity of the practice. People believe they are invoking one thing and are described as invoking another, which makes the question of what a person actually worships different from the question of what they intend. The claim to a fixed share then presents this as an arrangement with structure rather than random temptation.

crossReferences.why: Names the deities of the region directly and asks whether such attributions carry any authority.
Records the same claim in fuller form, with the directions from which the approach comes.
Continues the quoted claim into specific practices, and closes on what is lost by it.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you actually turn to first when something goes wrong: a person, a screen, a substance, a plan. Not what you would say you rely on. The passage distinguishes between the two, and simply naming your own first reflex accurately is most of the work it is asking for.

studies.title: Altering What Was Made
studies.meaning: The quoted claim continues through four verbs, each intensified in Arabic: misleading, filling with expectation, and then two instructions that lead to acts. Slitting the ears of livestock refers to a known practice of marking animals dedicated to a shrine. Altering the creation of God is far broader, and the commentators record a genuine range of readings for it rather than settling on any one.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators explain the reference to cattle by a pre-Islamic practice in which certain animals were marked by cutting their ears and then set aside from ordinary use, dedicated to a shrine. The Quran addresses that custom elsewhere as well. The passage quotes a claim rather than narrating events, which is how the classical commentaries read its structure.

keyTerms.gloss: I will fill them with wishes
keyTerms.note: An intensive verb from the root for a wish or a hope. It names the manufacture of expectation, which the following ayah then calls delusion, and the two are linked deliberately.
An intensive verb for cutting through something. It refers to marking livestock by cutting their ears, a practice by which an animal was dedicated and removed from ordinary use.
A phrase covering both the act of creating and the thing created. Commentators record a wide range of readings for what altering it means, and they preserve that range rather than resolving it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Livestock were the visible wealth of a family, and marking them was ordinary practice: a cut in the ear identified an owner across shared grazing ground. Dedicating an animal to a shrine used the same technique for another purpose, and the animal then could not be ridden, milked or slaughtered. Wealth was withdrawn from use by a single cut.
studies.didYouKnow: The four verbs in this quoted claim all carry the same emphatic ending in Arabic, one after another, which makes the passage sound like a formal oath. Commentators note the construction: what is reported is not a plan described but a vow spoken, and the grammar preserves its tone exactly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sequence moves from inward states to outward acts, beginning with misleading and expectation and ending with things done to animals and to creation itself. That order is the claim's own logic: what people do follows from what they have been led to expect. The passage then closes by naming the outcome as loss, in commercial language, rather than as punishment.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same practices of setting animals aside, and says God ordained none of them.
Continues immediately, naming the promises as delusion and their end as no escape.
Names the original disposition on which people were made, and says it does not change.

studies.applyIt: Notice something you have been told to want that you never actually chose: an expectation about a house, a body, a career, a timeline. Trace where it came from. This passage puts the manufacture of expectation before any action, and most of what follows is much easier to see once the source has been named.

studies.title: Promises That Are Delusion
studies.meaning: Two verbs summarise everything before them: he promises, and he fills with expectation. Then the whole is named with a word for something that deceives by looking better than it is. Commentators note that the word covers being taken in by an appearance rather than by an outright lie, which is why nothing here is stated as false. The second ayah gives the end point, and adds that no escape is found.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage that began with the boundary around forgiveness and ran through a quoted claim. Commentators treat these two ayat as the summary rather than as new material, and note that the surah immediately follows them with the matching description of those who believe, so the pair is never left standing alone.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for making a promise, used across the Quran of God's promises as well. Its neutrality is what pushes the evaluation into the following clause rather than into the verb.
From a root about being taken in by how something looks. It names deception that works through the appearance of a thing rather than through any false statement about it.
A noun of place from a verb meaning to swerve away from something. It names a route out that a person looks for and does not find, rather than a door that has been closed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A mirage in that landscape was a daily fact rather than a poetic image. Travellers saw water where none existed, and experienced guides learned to distrust their own eyes at certain hours of the day. The vocabulary of being deceived by appearance came from that, and nobody hearing it needed the comparison explained.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for delusion used here appears throughout the Quran, often in the phrase describing this life as the enjoyment of deception. Its root concerns being taken in by how something looks, so the Quran's ordinary term for a false promise is a word about appearance rather than about lying.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not say the promises are broken; it says they deceive. That is a finer point, and the commentators keep it: what is offered may even arrive and still fail, because the appearance that made it desirable was never accurate. The following ayah then sets the matching promise from God beside it, so the two are meant to be compared.

crossReferences.why: Sets the matching promise beside this one and asks who is more truthful in speech.
Warns that worldly life should not deceive you, nor the deceiver deceive you about God.
Records a speech at the end admitting that a promise was made and then not kept.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you are currently working toward and describe, in concrete detail, what the day after getting it will actually look like. Not the feeling, the day. This passage distinguishes a promise from an appearance, and that description is the simplest test available for telling which one you are holding.

studies.title: The Promise Of God Is True
studies.meaning: The matching description, placed deliberately against the one before it, and its distinctive element is the ending. Gardens and permanence are described in familiar terms, and then the sentence stops to characterise the promise itself as true, before closing with a question about whose speech is more truthful. So the passage argues about the reliability of the promise rather than adding anything to its content.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately following the description of promises that deceive. Commentators read the two as a single construction: a false promise is named, then a true one is set beside it with its truthfulness made explicit. The surah has used this technique earlier, giving two outcomes in adjacent ayat, though here the comparison is between promises rather than destinations.

keyTerms.note: A construction that restates the preceding sentence and then affirms it, a form Arabic uses to close an argument. It halts the description in order to characterise what has just been described.
One word covering truth, reality and a rightful claim together. Applied to a promise it means both that it corresponds to what will happen and that it is genuinely owed.
A verbal noun from the verb to say, used rarely in the Quran. Its choice makes the closing question about the act of speaking rather than about the content of what is said.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Promises in a society without writing were secured by reputation alone. A man's word was assessed by his record, and people traded on that assessment much as a modern person relies on a contract. Asking who is more truthful in speech was therefore a practical question, put in the exact terms that society used to decide whom to trust.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing question of this ayah appears earlier in the same surah in almost identical form, with one word exchanged for a near synonym. The tradition notes such paired questions, and here the repetition applies the same test twice: once about a report and once about a promise.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The weight of a promise is attached to the character of whoever makes it rather than to its content. Anyone can describe a garden; the question is whether the description is backed by anything. That is a claim about the grounds of hope, locating it in the speaker rather than in the attractiveness of what is offered, which is precisely how the preceding false promise failed.

crossReferences.why: Describes the promises this ayah is set against, and names them as delusion.
Asks the same closing question earlier in this surah, about a report rather than a promise.
Names the promise of God and states that God does not fail in what He has promised.

studies.applyIt: Think about how you actually decide to trust a promise. Usually it is the person's record rather than the offer itself. Apply that same test consciously to something you were promised recently and are hesitating over. This ayah does exactly that, in public, and the method it uses is the one you already have.

studies.title: Not According To Wishes
studies.meaning: Two sets of expectations are named and set aside together, one belonging to the community being addressed and one to those who received earlier scripture. Neither claim of standing settles anything. What follows is a plain statement of consequence for wrongdoing, and the absence of any protector besides God. Commentators note the even-handedness: the ayah levels a claim made by its own audience before it levels anyone else's.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a section arguing about who stands where before God. Commentators report that the ayah arrived amid competing claims of favour between religious communities in Medina, and that both are addressed inside one sentence. The reports describe an atmosphere of such claims rather than one occasion, which the tradition treats as its setting.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a wish, from the root used a few ayat earlier of manufactured expectation. Its reuse ties this ayah to the passage about false promises just above it.
A passive form from the root for a matched return. The passive leaves the agent unnamed, which puts the emphasis on the certainty of the return rather than on who delivers it.
The same pair used earlier in this surah inside a prayer asking God for both. Here their absence is stated, which turns that earlier request into the measure of what is lacking.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in Arabia was inherited and asserted. A family's claim to precedence was recited, defended and believed, and it genuinely affected how a person was treated. Religious communities in Medina held claims of a similar shape about their relationship with God. The ayah addresses a habit of thought that was entirely ordinary rather than an unusual arrogance.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for wishes in this ayah comes from the same root as the verb used a few ayat earlier for filling people with expectations. The surah is building a vocabulary across the passage, so a word first applied to deception is then applied to a community's own assumptions about itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies that belonging settles anything, and it does so symmetrically, naming its own audience's expectations first. That order matters: what is being made is not a claim about another community but a claim about claims. What replaces them is a plain account of consequence, with no protector named besides God, which returns the question to what a person actually did.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately with what does count, and specifies that it applies to male and female alike.
Answers a claim about who enters the Garden by asking for the evidence behind it.
States that whoever does good does it for himself, and your Lord is not unjust to servants.

studies.applyIt: Notice the claim you quietly rely on: that you are basically a good person, that your family is decent, that your community is on the right side. None of those are lies. The ayah simply removes them from the accounting and asks what you did, which is a narrower and far more useful question.

studies.title: Abraham, Taken As A Friend
studies.meaning: What actually counts is stated with an explicit clause: righteous work, from male or female, joined to belief. Nothing else is admitted, and nothing at all is deducted. The second ayah then asks who is better in religion and answers with three things together: submitting one's face wholly, doing good, and following Abraham's way. It closes with a description of Abraham the tradition has treated as his defining title.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the ayah that set aside competing claims of standing. The mention of Abraham does specific work in that context, since the communities disputing traced themselves to him. Commentators note this as the surah's second return to Abraham, and read both occurrences as answering claims of inherited precedence by pointing back to a shared ancestor.

keyTerms.note: The face stands for the whole person and for the direction one is turned. Submitting it means orienting everything, which is why the phrase is stronger than any English word for belief.
A word for turning aside from what surrounds one, toward what is straight. The Quran uses it almost exclusively of Abraham, and it describes a stance rather than a doctrine.
From a root about something entering into every gap, so the friendship is described as having penetrated completely. It is rarer and more intimate than the ordinary Arabic word for a friend.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Friendship in Arabia was a formal relationship carrying obligations, closer to alliance than to affection. A man's close friends were expected to defend him, house him and speak for him. Naming Abraham as God's friend used a word that carried all of that, in a society where such a bond was declared publicly and long remembered.
studies.didYouKnow: The title given to Abraham at the end of this ayah, God's close friend, became the name of a city and remains the ordinary Arabic name for Hebron. A single word from this ayah passed into geography, and is still used daily by people who may not know where it came from.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The first ayah removes gender from the account entirely, stating the condition and then naming both explicitly, which commentators read as answering an assumption rather than making a new claim. The second then defines religion by three things, all of them dispositions or actions, and none of them membership. A question about standing is answered by describing conduct.

crossReferences.why: Sets aside the claims of standing that these two ayat replace with conduct instead.
Describes Abraham as a community in himself, upright and not among those who associate.
Names believing men and believing women in parallel across a long list of qualities.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you do well and ask whether you would still do it if nobody could tell which group you belonged to. The passage strips membership out of the question entirely and leaves conduct standing. That is uncomfortable in a useful way, because it removes the part of an identity that requires no effort.

studies.title: Encompassing Every Thing
studies.meaning: A short ayah with two clauses. Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, and God encompasses everything. Commentators note the pairing of ownership with encompassment: the first is a claim about whom things belong to, the second about a knowledge that surrounds rather than observes. Placed after a long argument about standing, the ayah answers it by describing the scale on which such questions are settled.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the section that dealt with competing claims of favour and with what actually counts. Commentators read short ayat of this kind as punctuation within a long surah, marking the end of an argument by lifting the frame. No specific occasion is reported. The same statement recurs several times in the surah's later sections.

keyTerms.note: The preposition of possession placed first in the sentence, which Arabic uses for emphasis. Putting the owner before what is owned makes the ownership the point rather than the inventory.
From a root meaning to enclose on all sides, used of a wall around a garden. It appears earlier in this surah too, there describing knowledge of what people arrange in secret.
A phrase using the word for a thing in its widest sense, covering objects, events and states alike. Its indefiniteness is what makes the encompassment total rather than a long list.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ownership in that world was established by continuous possession and by the memory of neighbours. A man held land because his father had held it and everyone said so. There was no register, so ownership was fundamentally a matter of what a community knew. A statement joining possession to complete knowledge used exactly that logic, at the largest scale.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God recurs several times in the later sections of this surah, functioning almost as a refrain. Long surahs in the Quran often mark their divisions this way, with a short universal statement set between passages on very different subjects.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Joining ownership to encompassment answers a specific worry. An owner might not know what he owns, and a knower might have no claim on what he knows; putting the two together closes both gaps. After a long argument about who stands where, the ayah relocates the question: standing is not negotiated between parties but held inside a single knowledge.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for encompassing, there of God's knowledge of what is arranged in secret.
States the same ownership and adds that God will call to account for what is within you.
Closes by saying that God has encompassed every single thing in His knowledge.

studies.applyIt: When you next feel your situation is unseen, take the second clause of this ayah literally. The image is not of being watched from a distance but of being inside something. Sit with that for a minute rather than reasoning about it. The difference between those two pictures is most of what the ayah offers.

studies.title: They Ask You About Women
studies.meaning: A question is put and the answer redirects it. God answers, and so does what is already being recited in the Book, which commentators read as pointing back to the surah's opening ayat about orphan girls. Three groups are then named together: women whose due is withheld while marriage to them is desired, children rendered powerless, and orphans generally. The closing clause turns from obligation to whatever good is actually done.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Commentators report that questions about the arrangements set out at the start of this surah continued to be brought forward, and that this passage answers them by directing attention back to what had already been given. The situation described, a guardian withholding a ward's property while wanting to marry her, is the one the surah opened by addressing.

keyTerms.note: A verb for requesting a formal opinion on a difficult matter. Its use marks the question as one people had genuinely puzzled over rather than a casual query put in passing.
The passive of the verb to write, used of what has been appointed. Describing a woman's due as written places it outside the discretion of whoever happens to be holding it.
From the root for giving each party its due portion. The same root appeared in this surah's third ayah, so the answer closes on the word the whole question began from.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A guardian holding an orphan girl's property faced a real temptation with no oversight at all. Marrying her kept the property inside the household and avoided any handover. Everyone knew such arrangements existed, and the community had clearly kept asking about the boundaries, which is exactly what the verb opening this ayah records.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah refers the questioners back to what is already being recited in the Book, which commentators identify as the surah's own opening ayat. It is one of the places where the Quran points at itself as an existing text with earlier passages, in the middle of a surah still being revealed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer's shape is instructive: a question about entitlement is answered by naming the people most likely to be overlooked, and then by widening to any good done at all. That prevents the matter from resolving into a technical settlement. It also treats a repeated question as evidence that something already given had not been acted on.

crossReferences.why: Opens the surah with the same situation, guardians and the orphan girls in their care.
Establishes that an orphan's property must reach the orphan, which this question circles back to.
Names the powerless among men, women and children in the same grouping used here.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you keep asking a question you have already been answered. It usually means the answer requires something you would rather not do. Pick the one you have been circling and act on the part of it you already understand, which is generally most of it.

studies.title: Reconciliation Is Better
studies.meaning: The situation from earlier in the surah is stated from the other side: a wife fearing a breach or a withdrawal from her husband. What follows is not a procedure but a permission, that the two may settle matters between themselves, with a short judgement attached: settlement is better. Then an unusual observation about human nature, that souls are made present to grasping, which commentators read as explaining why settlement is hard.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, near the close of the surah's treatment of marriage. Commentators report cases of women whose husbands had withdrawn from them and who preferred an arrangement to a separation, and read the ayah as making room for such settlements. The reports describe more than one such case, agreeing that the passage arose from real arrangements rather than a hypothetical.

keyTerms.note: The same word used earlier in this surah of a wife. Its application here to a husband is what allows the tradition to read the two passages as one subject seen from both sides.
From the verb for averting the face. It names something less than a breach: the quiet removal of attention a marriage can survive on paper while failing in fact.
A word for holding tightly combined with wanting more, stronger than ordinary miserliness. The ayah says souls are brought into its presence, describing it as a condition rather than a choice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman whose husband had withdrawn had few options. Separation returned her to her father's people, often with children and always with reduced standing, and a second marriage was harder to arrange. An arrangement in which she kept the household while conceding something was frequently the outcome she herself preferred, and this ayah makes room for it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about souls being made present to grasping is quoted widely in Arabic as a description of human nature. It is grammatically passive, so the tendency is described as something brought to the soul rather than produced by it, and commentators read that construction as diagnostic rather than condemning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does something unusual by naming the obstacle in the same breath as the recommendation. Settlement is better, and here is why you will resist it. That combination treats moral instruction as needing a psychology and not only a standard, and it declines to pretend that what is recommended will feel natural to either party.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a breach when the fear is a husband's, earlier in this surah.
Sets out arbitration by both families, another route through the same difficulty.
Names those protected from their own grasping as the ones who genuinely succeed.

studies.applyIt: Think about a relationship you have kept formally intact while quietly withdrawing your attention from it. This ayah names that withdrawal as a distinct thing, separate from open conflict, and treats it as something the other person can feel. Give an hour of real attention back this week, without announcing that you are doing it.

studies.title: Left Hanging In Between
studies.meaning: A concession about what is not achievable, followed by an instruction about what is. Perfect evenness is stated as beyond reach even for someone who wants it, and commentators read that as concerning the heart rather than conduct. What is asked instead is not to lean so completely that someone is left suspended, neither held nor released. The second ayah then addresses separation and promises provision to both parties from God's abundance.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's treatment of marriage. Commentators read the first of these two ayat alongside the surah's third, where fairness was made the condition, and note that this one concedes the limit of what fairness can mean. No specific occasion is reported. The passage completes a sequence that began at the surah's very opening.

keyTerms.note: From a root for eager desire and greedy effort. The concession is made against maximum effort, so what is described as impossible is impossible even for someone genuinely trying at it.
A passive participle from the verb to suspend. It pictures a person hung between two states, neither in a marriage nor out of one, unable to move in either direction.
From the root for width and room. Closing the second ayah with it answers the fear behind staying in a failed marriage, which is that separation would leave someone with nothing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman neither divorced nor attended to had no standing anywhere. She could not remarry, could not return fully to her father's household, and had no claim she was able to press. The word this ayah uses for hanging described exactly that position, and it was common enough that the language already had a term for it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for being left suspended appears only here in the Quran, and it became the standard term in later Arabic for a woman in that precise situation. A single word from this ayah gave the language its way of naming a condition it had previously described only by circumstance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates feeling from conduct and asks only for the second, which is a specific claim about what can be required of a person. It concedes an inequality of the heart and then draws a line where that inequality damages somebody. The promise of provision after separation then removes the fear that most often keeps such situations frozen in place.

crossReferences.why: Makes fairness the condition at the surah's opening, whose limit this ayah then defines.
Asks for good company, and warns that dislike may conceal something genuinely good.
Addresses provision at separation, another passage assuming responsibility continues past an ending.

studies.applyIt: Look for a situation you are keeping suspended: a decision half made, a person half included, a job you have neither committed to nor left. The specific harm this ayah names is not the failure but the suspension. Resolve one of them this week in either direction, and notice which way you actually went.

studies.title: God Is In No Need
studies.meaning: A statement of ownership frames an instruction and then repeats itself after it, which is the ayah's whole structure. Between the two occurrences lies one instruction given to earlier communities and to this one alike: be mindful of God. Then the alternative is met not with a threat but with a shrug, since the ownership stands either way. The closing names describe God as self-sufficient and praiseworthy together.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the sequence of short universal statements that punctuate the surah's later sections. Commentators note that the instruction is described as having been given to those who received scripture before, which places this community inside a continuity rather than at a beginning. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah itself.

keyTerms.note: From the root for making a bequest, used earlier in this surah of inheritance. The same verb covers a will and a divine charge, both being something entrusted to be carried out.
From a root meaning to be free of need, which also gives the word for wealth. Applied to God it removes any suggestion that the instruction serves the one who gave it.
A form meaning worthy of praise, which is not the same as praised. It describes a quality holding whether or not anyone actually offers the praise, which suits this ayah's argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A patron in Arabia gave in order to be praised, and praise was the return he expected. Poets were paid to deliver it and its absence was an insult. Naming God as both in no need and worthy of praise separated two things that always travelled together in that society, and the separation would have been immediately noticeable.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement about the heavens and the earth appears twice inside this single ayah, once before the instruction and once after the alternative. Commentators note the repetition as the ayah's argument in structural form: nothing about the ownership changes depending on what anybody decides to do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage removes any suggestion that God gains from being obeyed. Ownership is stated before the instruction and again after refusal, unchanged, so the instruction cannot be a demand made for the sake of the one issuing it. That relocates the whole matter: mindfulness is described as something given for the benefit of whoever practises it.

crossReferences.why: States that if all on earth were ungrateful, God would still be free of need and praiseworthy.
Uses the same statement of ownership a few ayat earlier, inside a different argument.
Names people as those in need of God, and God as free of need and praiseworthy.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your practice is quietly transactional, done in the expectation of something arriving. This ayah cuts that wire twice inside one sentence. Try one act of devotion this week deliberately expecting nothing from it, and watch how strange that feels. The strangeness is informative.

studies.title: The Reward Of This World
studies.meaning: Three short ayat, each cutting from a different angle. Ownership again, with God named as the one entrusted with affairs. Then the capacity to remove an entire people and bring others, stated flatly. Then the sharpest of the three: whoever wants only this world's reward should note that both rewards are with God. Commentators read that as exposing a bad trade rather than condemning the desire itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the sequence of short statements that punctuate the surah's later sections. Commentators read the three together as a single movement, each ayah widening the frame further from the community's immediate concerns. The section follows a long passage on marriage and precedes one on those whose loyalty was divided.

keyTerms.note: A word for someone appointed to handle affairs on another's behalf. Used of God it describes an active role rather than observation, which is why it closes a statement about ownership.
A causative from the verb to go. It describes removal with no violence in the word itself, which makes the statement one about capacity rather than about anger.
From a root meaning to come back, related to the word for a garment one returns to wearing. Reward is pictured as something that comes back rather than something handed over.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A trader who took a certain small profit rather than waiting for a larger one was making a judgement everyone in Mecca and Medina understood. Caravans were financed on exactly that calculation. The argument in the third of these ayat is put in the terms of that trade: the smaller return was available inside the larger one all along.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for reward here is related to the Arabic for a garment, through a root meaning to return. Clothing was what a person came back to at the end of a day, and the same root produced a word for what comes back to someone as a consequence of what they did.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The three ayat build an argument by scale: ownership, then replaceability, then a choice about what to want. Placing the capacity to replace a people between the two makes the final point land differently, since someone choosing the smaller reward does so from a position that was never as secure as it felt. Desire is not condemned, only its aim.

crossReferences.why: Opens this sequence with the same statement of ownership and the same self-sufficiency.
Says whoever desires the harvest of the hereafter is increased in it, and gives the contrast.
Distinguishes those who want the fleeting from those who strive for the hereafter as believers.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you are chasing and ask what you would actually be giving up by aiming higher with the same effort. Not sacrifice, aim. The argument in the third of these ayat is about a trade being made badly, and most such trades are made without anyone noticing that they were trades.

studies.title: Witnesses Even Against Yourselves
studies.meaning: The demand is not to be just but to be one who stands up with justice, a form describing a posture maintained rather than an act performed. The hard cases are then named in order of difficulty: yourself, your parents, your relatives. A second temptation is anticipated, the pull towards whichever party seems more deserving of sympathy, and it is refused by saying God is nearer to both. The obstacle identified is desire, not ignorance.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the same section that dealt with a theft blamed on an innocent man, where the community's instinct had been to protect one of its own. The commentators read this ayah as generalising from that episode. Medina was a town of clans in which testimony was routinely shaped by loyalty, and an oath sworn for a kinsman was closer to a duty than to a lie.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the verb to stand, describing a standing role rather than a single stand. The same word is used of maintaining prayer, so it carries the sense of upholding something continuously.
A word tied to portions and shares, so the justice named is the kind that divides things fairly. Its own root can also carry deviation, and the form used here reverses that sense.
From a root for falling and for empty air. It names the pull of what one wants, pictured as a descent, which is why the ayah treats it as the thing that makes testimony swerve.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Justice in Arabia was tribal arithmetic. A killing was answered by a killing from the other clan, and a man who testified against his own people had cut the branch he sat on: protection, marriage prospects and trade all ran through kin. There was no state to appeal to if your family disowned you. Standing as a witness against a relative was nearer to exile than to inconvenience.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states this demand twice with its terms reversed. Here justice is the thing stood up for and God is the one witnessed to; at 5:8 the standing is for God and the witnessing is done with justice. The commentators note the mirroring, and the second passage names a different obstacle, hatred rather than desire.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice is grounded in something other than social benefit. The witness testifies to God, which makes accuracy a form of worship and removes the question of who is helped by the answer. The clause about rich and poor is the sharpest part: sympathy for the weak is no licence to bend a fact, and neither is deference to the strong. God is said to be nearer to both parties than the witness is.

crossReferences.why: States the same demand with the terms reversed, and names hatred as the pressure to resist.
Requires that speech be just even when a relative is involved.
Warns the Prophet against arguing for the treacherous, in the episode behind this passage.

studies.applyIt: The next time you retell an argument you were part of, include the strongest thing the other person said, in their words rather than your summary of it. You are not conceding anything. The ayah begins with testimony against yourself, and the smallest version of that is refusing to edit someone else's case when nobody would notice.

studies.title: Believe In All Of It
studies.meaning: The address is to people who already believe, and the command is to believe. The commentators offer a range: stay firm on it, deepen it, or accept what you have not yet acknowledged. The content is then listed as a chain, this Book and the Book sent before it, and the denial clause widens to angels, messengers and the Last Day. What is described is not a set of separate beliefs but one thing with parts, which is why rejecting any of them is called straying far.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a surah much concerned with people whose commitment was partial and with argument between communities holding earlier scriptures. The insistence on the Book sent before is not incidental in that setting. The commentators record no single occasion and read the address as directed at the community itself, whose belief was being asked to become something more than a stated position.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form suggesting descent in stages, used of the Quran's revelation over years. A plainer form appears in the same sentence for the earlier scripture, and the commentators note the difference.
Classical grammarians connect the word with a root for a message or an errand. Angels appear in the list of what may not be rejected, placed between God Himself and the scriptures He sent.
The verb for losing your road in open country where there are no landmarks. It is paired here with a word for distance, so error is measured as a length walked rather than a single wrong turn.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was a town where scriptural religion was already familiar. Jewish tribes had lived there for generations, kept their books, and their scholars were consulted about the past. Arabs in the oasis had grown up hearing of earlier prophets and of one still expected. A claim to continue that line was intelligible to everybody there in a way it had not been in Mecca.
studies.didYouKnow: Five things are named here as objects of belief, and the same five are gathered in the long ayah on righteousness in surah 2, where it is defined as belief in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets. The order differs between the two, and neither passage presents its list as exhaustive.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief is presented as something that can be commanded of believers, which means it is not treated as a state already completed. The list refuses a religion beginning with this messenger: earlier scripture is part of the content rather than a courtesy extended to others. And the closing image measures rejection as distance travelled, which implies that positions are arrived at gradually and can be walked back.

crossReferences.why: Gathers the same objects of belief, defining righteousness by them rather than by direction of prayer.
Shows the response, believers making no distinction between any of His messengers.
Names the same religion as enjoined on Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus alike.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the things you say you believe and ask what you did about it this month. Not whether you affirmed it, what you did. The ayah addresses people who had already said the words and asks them for the thing itself, which suggests the gap between saying and holding is normal rather than a scandal.

studies.title: Then Believed, Then Refused
studies.meaning: A sequence is recited: belief, refusal, belief, refusal, and then an increase in refusal. Five stages, and commentators note that what closes the door is the last one rather than the oscillation itself. The Quran elsewhere describes repentance as available after any single turning; here what is described is a pattern that has settled into a direction. The two things withheld are forgiveness and guidance to a way.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening a long section on those whose loyalty was divided. Commentators connect the ayah to people who moved back and forth as the community's fortunes rose and fell, and read the escalation at the end as describing where such movement finally arrives. No single occasion is reported, and the description is read as a pattern rather than a report.

keyTerms.note: A connective indicating sequence with an interval, unlike the ordinary word for and. Repeated four times here, it makes the ayah a chronology rather than a list of possible alternatives.
A reflexive form of the verb to increase, so the movement is described as self-generated. It marks the exact point where oscillation stops and a settled direction begins.
The ordinary word for a road. What is withheld is described as a route rather than as an outcome, so the loss named is the loss of a means rather than of a destination.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a city where the community's fortunes changed with each engagement, alignment was constantly reassessed. People adjusted their position quietly and repeatedly, and everyone could name someone who had. That constant recalculation is the behaviour this ayah traces, and its first hearers would have followed the sequence as a description of people they knew.
studies.didYouKnow: The word marking each stage of this ayah indicates a gap in time, not merely a sequence. Arabic distinguishes between events joined immediately and events separated by an interval, and the choice here means the ayah describes a whole life rather than one episode of confusion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The difficulty is located in a settled direction rather than in inconstancy as such. Four reversals are recited without comment; the fifth stage is what changes the sentence. That preserves the wide promise of repentance stated earlier in the surah, since what is described is not a person who wavered but one who stopped wavering in a particular direction.

crossReferences.why: Names the exit from this passage: repentance, reform, holding fast, and sincerity of religion.
Describes the wavering itself a few ayat later, as being with neither one party nor the other.
Says they believed and then rejected, so their hearts were sealed and they do not understand.

studies.applyIt: Notice a pattern you have repeated more than twice: the same resolution, the same collapse, the same restart. The ayah does not condemn the cycle. What it marks is the point where a person begins arguing for the collapse rather than resisting it. Check honestly which of those two you are currently doing.

studies.title: Where Glory Is Sought
studies.meaning: An announcement is made in the vocabulary of good news and applied to a painful punishment, and the reversal is deliberate. Then the people are identified by one behaviour, taking as allies those outside the community rather than those inside it, and a question is asked about the motive: do they seek standing there. The answer supplied is that all standing belongs to God, which relocates the object rather than condemning the desire.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the section on those whose loyalty was divided. Commentators describe people in the city maintaining relationships with the community's opponents as insurance, and read the question about honour as naming what such arrangements were really for. The setting is one where standing depended on visible association, which the passage addresses head on.

keyTerms.note: A verb used across the Quran for glad tidings, from a root about the skin showing a change. Attaching it to punishment is a deliberate inversion that commentators discuss at length.
From a root meaning rare, precious and inaccessible. It names the standing of someone who cannot be reached or humiliated, which is exactly what alliance was being sought to provide.
The plural of the word for a close ally used across this surah. It names a formal arrangement carrying obligations rather than friendship or ordinary social contact.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A person's safety in Arabia came from who would answer for them. Holding a relationship with a rising power was the standard hedge, pursued openly and without embarrassment. What this passage addresses is not treachery in the dramatic sense but the ordinary prudence of a society where standing had to be borrowed from somewhere else.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for announcing good news in this ayah is the same one used elsewhere in the Quran for the promise of a child and the promise of the Garden. Its inversion here is one of several places where the Quran uses a word against its usual sense, and commentators treat the effect as deliberate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The question asked is diagnostic rather than accusatory, since it names what people were actually seeking. The answer then does not tell them to stop wanting standing but says the whole of it lies elsewhere. That treats the failure as a misdirection rather than as an appetite to be suppressed, which is the same move the surah makes with wealth and with reward.

crossReferences.why: Restates the instruction directly to believers a few ayat later, in the form of a question.
Says whoever desires honour should know that all honour belongs to God entirely.
Records a claim that the mightier will expel the weaker, and answers that might belongs to God.

studies.applyIt: Ask where you go to feel that you count: a group, a title, an association you mention when introducing yourself. Not in order to give it up. Just name it accurately once. This passage's method is to identify the source you draw standing from, and naming it is most of what changes.

studies.title: Until They Change The Subject
studies.meaning: An instruction is recalled rather than issued, described as already revealed in the Book: do not remain seated where revelation is being rejected or mocked, until the conversation turns to something else. The condition is precise. It is the sitting that is addressed and not the speaking, and the reason given is that staying makes you like them. Commentators note that the exit is temporary and tied to the subject rather than to the company.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, referring back to an instruction given earlier, which commentators identify with a passage revealed in Mecca addressing the same situation. Its restatement here applies it to a different setting: a city where such conversations happened among neighbours rather than strangers, which made leaving costlier and far more visible than it had been before.

keyTerms.note: The verb for sitting, used earlier in this surah of those who stayed behind. It addresses physical presence rather than participation, which is what makes this instruction unusual.
A verb for stepping into water and stirring it up. Applied to speech it describes talk that goes in without care, which is how the Quran regularly names idle or mocking conversation.
A word for a likeness or an equivalent. The claim is not that you become guilty of what they said but that you occupy the same position, which is a claim about presence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gatherings in Medina were where a person's world was conducted: business, marriage arrangements, news. Leaving one visibly was a public act with consequences, and the people speaking were often relatives or trading partners. The instruction is costly in exactly the way its first hearers would have felt, which is why the exit lasts only as long as the subject.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction is described as already revealed, and commentators identify the earlier passage as a Meccan one addressing the same situation. This ayah is therefore one of the places where the Quran refers back to itself by content, treating an earlier revelation as a text the audience could be expected to recall.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Presence is treated as participation, which is a strong claim. Nothing needs to be said or agreed to; remaining seated is itself a position. The remedy is also made proportionate and temporary, tied to a subject rather than to people, which keeps it from becoming a general withdrawal from anyone whose speech one happens to dislike.

crossReferences.why: Gives the earlier instruction, to turn away from those who wade into ridicule of revelation.
Describes the servants of the Merciful as passing by idle talk with dignity intact.
Names what does have good in private conversation, a few ayat earlier in this surah.

studies.applyIt: Next time a conversation turns to something you would rather not be part of, do not argue and do not stay. Get up, refill something, take a call, come back when it has moved on. The instruction here concerns position rather than protest, and it is easier to follow than most people expect.

studies.title: Those Who Lie In Wait
studies.meaning: A behaviour is shown by quoting it twice. When the community succeeds, the claim is that they were with you; when the other side gains, the claim is that they protected you from the believers. Both sentences are questions, which is what makes them work as claims on somebody. The ayah then defers judgement to the Day of Resurrection and closes with a statement about what will never be granted.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the section on those whose loyalty was divided. Commentators describe people who stayed close to the community without committing to it, positioning themselves to claim credit whichever way an engagement went. The reports describe the behaviour as a recognised pattern in the city rather than one incident, and the passage records both of its halves.

keyTerms.note: A verb for waiting for something to happen to someone. It describes patience with a purpose, watching to see how a situation resolves before deciding where to stand.
From the verb to open. Victory in Arabic is named as an opening rather than as a conquest, which is why one word covers a decisive success and the unlocking of something closed.
A rare verb meaning to take control of something and dominate it. Its use inside a boast makes the claim awkward, since it concedes rather more than the speaker intends.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Between two contending powers, a small party's best strategy was to be owed something by both. Claims of past assistance were the currency of that position, and they were pressed loudly at exactly the moment they became payable. Everyone in Medina had watched such claims being made, usually within days of an outcome becoming clear.
studies.didYouKnow: Both claims in this ayah are phrased as questions rather than as statements, which in Arabic makes them harder to refuse. A question invites the hearer to supply the agreement, and commentators note that this construction is what makes the two sentences a strategy rather than merely a lie.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a final judgement against a present ambiguity: both claims may be difficult to disprove now, and the matter is deferred rather than settled. Then the closing clause does something different, promising that no way will be given over the believers, which the commentators discuss carefully as a statement about ultimate outcome.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same position from inside, wavering with neither one party nor the other.
Describes those who wait for misfortune to turn against the believers, and what awaits them.
Names those who hold others back and come to the fighting only very reluctantly.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you have positioned yourself so as to be able to claim credit either way. Everyone does this at work, in families, in arguments among friends. Pick one such position and commit to it out loud this week, before you know how it turns out. That is the whole of what the ayah describes.

studies.title: Standing Up Lazily
studies.meaning: An attempt at deception is described and answered in the same clause, using one verb of both parties, which the commentators discuss carefully as an instance of the Quran matching a word to itself rather than attributing deception to God. Then the description turns concrete: standing for prayer without energy, performing for an audience, and remembering God only a little. The diagnosis is delivered through posture.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the section on those whose loyalty was divided. Commentators note that the ayah moves from an abstract claim about deception to an observable behaviour, and read the description as one the community could verify for itself. The setting is a city where prayer was congregational and attendance was visible to everybody present.

keyTerms.note: A form implying attempt and reciprocity. Commentators stress that its use of God is a matching of the word to itself, a known Arabic device, rather than any attribution of deception.
A plural adjective for sluggishness. It describes the manner of standing rather than the fact of it, so the failure named is visible in how a body actually carries itself.
From the verb to see, in a reciprocal form. The audience is built into the word, so the act is described as performed toward people rather than merely observed by them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Prayer in Medina was performed together, in rows, several times a day. Absence was noticed and so was manner. In a congregation of neighbours, how a man stood was as legible as whether he came at all, and everyone could tell the difference between someone present and someone merely attending.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the same verb for the attempt at deception and for God's response, a construction Arabic employs to indicate a matching answer rather than an identical act. Commentators across the tradition explain this device carefully, and it appears wherever a response is described in the language of the offence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates a spiritual condition in a physical detail. Nothing is inferred from doctrine or from speech; the evidence offered is the way a person stands. That implies inner states have outward form, a claim with two edges, since it means a practice done listlessly is reporting something rather than merely being imperfect.

crossReferences.why: Names those heedless in their prayer, who perform it in order to be seen by people.
Says their spending is not accepted, and that they come to prayer only reluctantly.
Describes remembrance in every posture, which this ayah's description stands directly against.

studies.applyIt: Watch how you stand for prayer this week rather than what you say in it. Not in order to judge yourself. This ayah's diagnostic is physical, and posture is unusually honest: it reports what you actually brought before you have had time to decide what you meant to bring.

studies.title: Wavering Between The Two
studies.meaning: A single word carries the first ayah, an intensive form describing something driven back and forth, and the sentence then spells it out: not toward these, not toward those. The second ayah turns to believers with an instruction and a question. The question is the sharper half, asking whether they want to hand God a clear case against themselves, which frames the matter as evidence rather than as loyalty.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the passage on divided loyalty and then turning to address the community directly. Commentators note the shift: a description of others becomes an instruction to the hearers, so the ayat are read as a warning against becoming what has just been described. The setting is a city where such alliances were practically available to anyone.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from a root about swinging or dangling. It pictures something moved by an external force rather than choosing, like a bucket swinging inside a well shaft.
A word for authority and for the proof that establishes it. The question asks whether they wish to supply the evidence themselves, which turns the matter into one of testimony.
The plural of the word for a close ally, carrying formal obligations in that society. The instruction concerns alliance rather than acquaintance, as the surah's usage elsewhere makes clear.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A well bucket swung on its rope when it was neither at the water nor at the rim, and the word this ayah uses comes from that motion. Everyone drew water daily. The image would have arrived immediately: something suspended and moving, useful in neither position, and going wherever the rope was pulled.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing this wavering occurs only once in the Quran and is built from a doubled root, a form Arabic uses for repeated back-and-forth motion. Its sound carries the meaning, which is why translators reach for words like wavering, vacillating or dangling, none of which quite reproduce the effect.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The second ayah reframes the whole question as one of evidence. Rather than saying such alliance is disloyal, it asks whether a person wants to furnish a clear case against himself, which puts the hearer in the position of a witness testifying about his own life. That is a distinctive way of stating an instruction, addressing the will rather than the conscience.

crossReferences.why: Traces the sequence of reversals that ends in exactly this suspended position.
Names the same behaviour a few ayat earlier and asks what is really being sought in it.
Addresses the same matter of alliance, with an exception for those under real threat.

studies.applyIt: Identify one area where you have carefully avoided committing, so that you can move either way later. Notice what that flexibility costs you in energy, since holding two options open takes more than either would. Then close one this week. The ayah's image is of something that never comes to rest.

studies.title: Except Those Who Turn Back
studies.meaning: The lowest level of the Fire is named, using a word for a descending depth rather than a rank, and then the entire passage is opened by an exception. Four things are listed: repenting, setting things right, holding fast to God, and making one's religion sincerely His. Commentators note that the exception is placed immediately after the severest statement in the section, so the door opens at the point of greatest weight.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the long section on divided loyalty. Commentators read the exception as belonging to the same revelation rather than arriving later, and note that this surah consistently follows a severe statement with an opening. The people described had lived in the city throughout, so the exit named was practically available to exactly those the passage concerned.

keyTerms.note: A word for a step going down, the opposite of the term used for the ascending degrees promised earlier in this surah. The vocabulary of ranks is mirrored downward here.
From a root meaning to grasp something for protection, used of clinging to a rope. It describes an active grip rather than a belief, which is why it sits among verbs of doing.
From a root meaning to clear something of admixture, as metal is refined. Applied to religion it names the removal of other motives rather than the addition of any new thing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Refining metal was a familiar process: heating something until what was mixed in separated and could be drawn off. The word for sincerity comes from that, and its first hearers would have understood it as a subtraction rather than an addition. Nothing is added to make a thing pure; other things are taken out of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the lowest level of the Fire is a term for a descending step, and it mirrors the word for ascending degrees used earlier in this surah. The Quran builds both directions from the vocabulary of stairs, so a single architectural image runs upward and downward through the chapter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The four conditions of the exception move from inward to outward and back: turning, repairing, holding on, and purifying motive. Repentance alone is not the whole of it, and repair is named second, which keeps the turn from being purely private. The passage then places such people with the believers, restoring a standing rather than merely lifting a penalty.

crossReferences.why: Describes the pattern this exception releases people from, and its final settled direction.
States the terms of repentance earlier in this surah, in a more general form.
Uses the same verb for holding fast, there of holding to the rope of God together.

studies.applyIt: Take the four things named here in order and apply them to one thing you regret: turn from it, repair what you can, take hold of something steadier, and remove whatever other motive is still attached. The second and fourth are the ones people skip, and they are usually where the work actually is.

studies.title: What Would God Gain
studies.meaning: A question opens the passage and it is not rhetorical in the usual way: it asks what purpose punishment would serve for someone who is grateful and believes. Then two short instructions about speech and pardon, each closing on a divine name that matches it. What holds the three together is that God is described as appreciative, as hearing, and as pardoning while capable, so each instruction rests on something about God rather than on a rule.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the section on those whose loyalty was divided and turning toward a wider address. Commentators read the opening question as softening the severity of the passage preceding it. The allowance for someone wronged to speak openly is connected in some reports to disputes among neighbours, though no single occasion is agreed upon.

keyTerms.note: The word for a grateful person, applied here to God. Commentators read it as meaning that God acknowledges and multiplies what is small, since God receives nothing at all from anyone.
A noun for raising the voice or making something public. What is addressed is the broadcasting of harsh speech rather than the feeling behind it, which is why the exception concerns a grievance.
Two names paired deliberately. Pardon from someone unable to act is not pardon at all, so the second name is what gives the first its weight inside the sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A grievance in a small city had two possible routes: speak it publicly and force the matter into the open, or absorb it and let the relationship continue. Both were costly. The allowance given here for a wronged person to speak recognises that silence was not always available, and that some injuries had no other remedy.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for gratitude is applied to God in this passage, which the classical commentators discuss carefully. Since God gains nothing, they explain the name as describing how small acts are received and multiplied, and note that the Quran uses several human words this way while insisting the meaning is not identical.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The opening question relocates punishment from something owed to something purposive, and finds no purpose in it for a person who is grateful and believes. That reframes the subject: consequence is not described as satisfying anything in God. The three ayat then set a high standard for speech while allowing the wronged an exception, and close by naming pardon as the better option.

crossReferences.why: Permits an equivalent response, then names pardon and reconciliation as what God rewards.
States that gratitude brings increase, the other side of this passage's opening question.
Asks those with standing to pardon and overlook, since they want God's forgiveness themselves.

studies.applyIt: Take a grievance you have been telling people about. This passage does not say you were wrong to speak; it explicitly allows it. But it names pardon as the better option and attaches a name of God to that. Try one week of not raising it, and see what it costs you and what it does not.

studies.title: We Believe In Some
studies.meaning: A position is described precisely and then named. Some accept part of what was sent and reject the rest, separating God from His messengers, and look for a route somewhere between acceptance and refusal. Commentators note that the passage's concern is the middle path itself, described as a chosen position rather than as hesitation. The following ayah states the verdict, using the word for truly to close off any negotiation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening a section addressed to communities holding earlier scripture. Commentators place it among arguments in Medina about which messengers were to be accepted, in a city where several scriptural traditions lived side by side and each held a settled position on the others. No single occasion is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for splitting something into parts. Its object here is God and His messengers, so what is described is a division of things the passage treats as inseparable.
The ordinary word for a road. Describing the middle position as a path chosen makes it deliberate, which is why the following ayah can treat it as a settled stance.
A word covering truth and reality together. Attached to the verdict, it closes the gap between what a position calls itself and what it actually amounts to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Communities in Medina held long-settled views on which prophets belonged to their line and which did not, and these were part of a family's identity rather than an intellectual position. Accepting a new claim meant rearranging a great deal. The middle path described here was the natural way through, which is precisely why the passage addresses it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for separating between messengers appears in this passage and again in the very next ayah with a negation, so one word describes both the condemned position and the approved one within two sentences. The Quran often builds such a pair, defining a thing and its opposite by a single term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is treated as a single thing with many deliveries, so selecting among the messengers is described as rejecting the source rather than as partial acceptance. That is a claim about unity. It also refuses the middle position specifically, which is unusual, since middle positions are generally treated as caution rather than as a stance requiring a verdict.

crossReferences.why: States the approved position immediately after, using the same verb with a negation attached.
Describes believers as making no distinction between any one of God's messengers.
Lists the prophets by name and says we make no distinction between any of them.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you have quietly assembled a position out of the parts you found agreeable. Everyone does this with traditions, with advice, with medicine. Name one thing you have set aside because it was inconvenient rather than because you examined it, and look at it once, properly, this week.

studies.title: No Distinction Between Them
studies.meaning: The matching statement, built from the same verb as the ayah before it with a negation added. Those who believe in God and His messengers and draw no line between any of them are promised their recompense. Commentators note the shift in number, since the promise is stated for a group while the wage is owed to each. The closing names are forgiveness and mercy rather than any name of justice.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing the pair that began with the description of a selective belief. Commentators read the two ayat as a single construction, and note that this surah frequently states a position and then its opposite in adjacent ayat. The setting is a city where several scriptural communities lived alongside each other with settled views about one another.

keyTerms.note: The same intensive verb used in the previous ayah, now negated. Placing them together defines the approved position entirely by contrast with the one just described before it.
A word for a single individual, used in negative constructions to mean not even one. Its presence rules out drawing a line anywhere, however small the distinction being claimed.
The plural of the ordinary word for a wage. Its use keeps the promise inside the language of what is owed rather than of what is freely given as a favour.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Loyalty to a line of prophets was inherited in much the way loyalty to a tribe was, and it carried similar social weight. Being told that no distinction should be drawn among them cut across an inheritance people had been raised inside. The instruction was not abstract; it asked for a rearrangement of how a family understood itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states this principle of making no distinction among messengers in several places, and in two of them it appears as words spoken by the believers themselves rather than as an instruction given to them. The community is shown adopting the position rather than only being told to hold it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage closes on forgiveness and mercy rather than on any name concerning reward, which commentators find significant. A statement about correct belief ends by naming the attributes relevant to failure, which suggests the position described is not being treated as a qualification met but as an orientation that will still need covering.

crossReferences.why: Describes the position this ayah answers, selecting among messengers and seeking a path between.
Puts this same statement into the mouths of the believers, as words they say themselves.
Lists the prophets and closes with submission to God and no distinction among any of them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a tradition you inherited and the parts of it you were taught to hold at arm's length. Not doctrine necessarily, just the figures and sources your family or community quietly discounted. Read something from one of them this week, on its own terms, before deciding anything about it.

studies.title: Show Us God Plainly
studies.meaning: A demand for a book sent down from the sky is answered by pointing to a larger demand made long before, and that comparison is the whole argument. Commentators note that the passage does not refuse the request directly; it places it inside a history. Two episodes follow, the demand to see God and the making of the calf, and both close with something unexpected: a pardon, and an authority given.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section addressed to communities holding earlier scripture. Commentators report that a demand was put to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) for a written text delivered from the sky in the manner described in earlier scripture. The reports differ over who made it and agree on its substance, and the ayah answers by recalling episodes from the account of Moses.

keyTerms.note: The same root used a few ayat earlier of speaking aloud. Here it means seeing with the eyes rather than being told, so the demand is for direct perception with nothing in between.
A word for a lightning strike and for the stupor it causes. It names both the event and its effect, which is why commentators discuss whether it describes death or a loss of consciousness.
From the root meaning to erase a trace. Its placement after the calf, the gravest episode named, is what makes the sentence turn, since pardon rather than punishment closes the account.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A written document carried enormous authority in a largely oral society, precisely because it was rare. Communities with scripture were known as people of the Book, and the physical text was part of their standing. Asking for a book delivered from the sky was a demand for the one thing that could settle a dispute about authority in public.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran returns to the account of Moses more often than to any other narrative, and its retellings vary in detail from one place to another according to the argument being made. Here two separate episodes are compressed into a single ayah, because the point being made is comparative rather than narrative.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A demand for a sign is answered by observing what happened when larger signs were given. That is an argument about the relation between evidence and conviction: the calf came after clear proofs, so proof is shown not to produce belief on its own. And the account closes with pardon and with authority given, which keeps the history from being simply an indictment.

crossReferences.why: Narrates the same demand to see God plainly, and what followed immediately from it.
Gives the episode of the calf at greater length, including the turning that followed it.
Says a written text sent down in their hands would still have been called plain magic.

studies.applyIt: Notice what evidence you have told yourself would settle a question you keep reopening. Then ask whether the last piece of evidence that arrived actually settled anything. This passage's argument is that the demand usually outlives the answer, which is worth testing against your own history first.

studies.title: The Mountain Raised Above
studies.meaning: Three moments are set side by side, each attached to a pledge: the mountain raised over them, an instruction to enter a gate humbly, and an instruction about the Sabbath. Commentators discuss the first at length and record differing readings of what the raising describes. What binds the three is the closing word, a covenant called thick and heavy, using the same phrase this surah applied earlier to a marriage.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the address to communities holding earlier scripture. Commentators read the ayah as a compressed recollection of episodes narrated at greater length elsewhere in the Quran, gathered here because each involves a pledge. The passage sits between a response to a demand for a sign and a list of covenant failures, so its subject is what was undertaken.

keyTerms.note: A word the Quran uses specifically of the mountain of Moses. Commentators record differing readings of what its raising over them describes, and they preserve the range rather than settling it.
A plural participle describing the manner of entering. It names a posture rather than an action performed once inside, so the instruction concerns how a threshold is crossed.
The same phrase this surah used earlier of a marriage. Its reuse here for a community's pledge places a household agreement and a covenant with God inside one vocabulary.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A pledge in Arabia was sworn publicly, often with a physical act attached: hands clasped, a stone touched, a formula repeated before witnesses. Its binding force came from having been seen. The episodes recalled here each attach a pledge to a place or an act, which would have read to that audience as the proper shape of a covenant.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a solid covenant occurs only a few times in the Quran: of the pledge taken from the prophets, of a marriage, and here of a community's undertaking. Commentators note that three very different bonds are described by one term, which is the sort of link a long surah builds deliberately.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage gathers instructions of different kinds under a single idea, which is that something was undertaken. Entering a gate, observing a day, and accepting a covenant at a mountain are not similar acts; what makes them one subject is the pledge attached to each. That treats the moral life as a matter of standing agreements rather than of separate rules.

crossReferences.why: Narrates the raising of the mountain and the covenant taken there at greater length.
Gives the instruction about entering the gate, and reports what was said instead.
Uses the same phrase for a solid covenant, there of the pledge inside a marriage.

studies.applyIt: Make a short list of what you have actually undertaken: promises you gave, roles you accepted, things you said you would be. Not aspirations, undertakings.
