Most people find the list shorter and heavier than they expected, and simply having it written down changes which of them get kept.

studies.title: Our Hearts Are Covered
studies.meaning: A series of covenant failures is listed, and one item is a phrase they said about themselves: our hearts are wrapped. The reply reverses the claim's direction, saying it is God who sealed them, and commentators read the exchange as concerning causation rather than the condition itself. A second charge follows, a grave falsehood spoken against Mary, which the Quran names without ever repeating it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the address to communities holding earlier scripture. Commentators explain the phrase about wrapped hearts as an idiom in use at the time, a claim that a message could not get through. The passage lists specific failures rather than making a general accusation, and it ends with the qualification that a few among them do believe.

keyTerms.note: A plural adjective from a root meaning a covering or a sheath. The claim describes hearts as already enclosed, turning an unwillingness to hear into a condition nobody could be blamed for.
The verb for pressing a seal into clay or wax. It describes a closure that is fixed rather than temporary, and commentators read it as following repeated refusal rather than as an original state.
From a root meaning to leave someone stunned. The same word appeared earlier in this surah, of a husband reclaiming a dowry and of blaming an innocent person for a fault.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A sword kept in a sheath was described with the same word used here of the heart. The image was ordinary rather than poetic: something serviceable but covered, unavailable until drawn. Claiming that one's heart was sheathed used a picture people handled daily, which is part of why the reply engages the image rather than dismissing it.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran does not repeat the falsehood spoken against Mary; it names it as a great slander and moves on. Commentators note this restraint, and observe that the Quran elsewhere devotes a long passage to Mary's account, so the refusal to restate the charge here is a choice rather than a gap.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exchange about hearts turns on who did the covering. A claim of incapacity is met not by denial but by relocating its cause, which preserves responsibility while conceding the condition. The list also stays specific, naming acts rather than a people, and closes with an exception for the few, which commentators consistently emphasise when reading it.

crossReferences.why: Records the same claim about wrapped hearts, and gives the same answer to it.
Gives the account of Mary at length, including the defence that was made of her.
Continues the list with the next claim, this one concerning the Messiah himself.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you say you cannot change something about yourself. Sometimes that is accurate. But listen to the sentence you use, and ask whether it describes a condition or excuses one. The passage does not deny that hearts can close. It disputes only the account of how they got that way.

studies.title: It Was Made To Appear
studies.meaning: A claim is quoted and then denied twice, at the beginning of the sentence and again at its end. What the Quran states is that he was neither killed nor crucified, and that the matter was made to appear otherwise. The classical commentators offer several accounts of how, and set them side by side without agreement. The ayah describes those who differ as in doubt, following conjecture rather than knowledge.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within a passage listing claims made about earlier prophets. The community in Medina lived among people with settled traditions about Jesus, and Christian communities across the region held the crucifixion as central to their faith. Commentators read the ayah as addressing a claim of having accomplished the killing, and the tradition has always understood it as denying that outcome.

keyTerms.note: A title the Quran uses of Jesus throughout, never as a description it disputes. It appears here inside the quoted claim and is left standing rather than corrected in any way.
A passive from the root for likeness and ambiguity. The grammar leaves the subject unnamed, which is why commentators offer several readings and none can claim the ayah's own words.
A word for an opinion held without certainty. It stands against knowledge in the same sentence, so the charge concerns the basis of a claim rather than the sincerity of those making it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Christian communities were established across Arabia and beyond it, in Najran, in Syria and in Abyssinia, and the community in Medina had direct contact with them. A delegation from Najran later came to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) for discussion. Claims about Jesus were not distant theology in that setting; they were the subject of conversations people actually had.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names Jesus as the Messiah repeatedly and describes his birth, his signs and his message at length, and this ayah calls him the Messenger of God inside the very claim it is denying. What is denied is the outcome asserted, and the titles standing inside the quoted sentence are left untouched.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies an outcome and then declines to specify a mechanism, which is why the classical commentaries record several accounts rather than one. What it affirms positively arrives in the following ayah: he was raised to God. Christians have understood the matter differently, and the difference is a real one that this ayah itself describes as something people dispute.

crossReferences.why: States what the Quran affirms positively, that God raised him up to Himself.
Records God taking him and raising him, in another passage on the same subject.
Places peace on him at his birth, at his death, and on the day he is raised alive.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you hold a firm position on something you have never examined, simply because the people around you hold it. The charge in this ayah concerns the basis of a claim rather than its content. Pick one such position of your own and find out, this week, what it actually rests on.

studies.title: Raised Up To Himself
studies.meaning: What the passage affirms is stated in four words: rather, God raised him to Himself. Nothing further is described, and commentators note the restraint. The second ayah then makes a statement about belief coming before a death, and the tradition preserves genuinely different readings of whose death is meant, some taking it as his and some as each individual at their own end.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing the passage about claims made concerning Jesus. Commentators read the two ayat as the positive counterpart to the denial before them. The second has been discussed extensively in the tradition, since its pronouns can be read more than one way, and the classical commentaries transmit the alternatives without choosing between them.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for raising something up, used of rank as well as of position. The Quran leaves the manner unspecified, which is why commentators discuss it without claiming the ayah settles it.
A possessive pronoun that can attach to either party in the sentence. That ambiguity is the source of the tradition's two readings, and the commentaries record both rather than resolving it.
From the root for presence. A witness testifies to what he was there for, so the word implies a relationship to those being testified about rather than the role of a judge over them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the instrument of justice in a world without records, and a witness was chosen for standing rather than for neutrality. Being testified about by somebody who knew you was the most serious form of accountability available. That is the picture the second ayah draws on, and its first hearers would have felt the weight immediately.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these two ayat contains a pronoun that can attach to two different subjects, and the classical commentaries record both readings side by side across the centuries. It is one of the clearest examples of the tradition transmitting a genuine grammatical ambiguity rather than resolving it into one account.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The affirmation is deliberately brief where the denial before it was emphatic, which shapes what the passage claims to know. The closing names, mighty and wise, are attached to a raising rather than to a punishment, so the event is described as an exercise of power under judgement. The witness in the second ayah returns the matter to accountability.

crossReferences.why: States the denial this ayah answers, and the two are read together throughout the tradition.
Describes God taking him and raising him, and placing his followers above those who refused.
Shows him questioned about what he told people, answering that God was the witness over them.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much more confidently you speak about things you were told than about things you saw. This passage is unusually careful about that difference, affirming little and denying firmly. Try marking the distinction once this week, out loud, when you pass something on: what you know, and what you heard.

studies.title: Good Things Withheld
studies.meaning: A consequence is described as following from conduct: because of wrongdoing, and because of turning many away from God's path, things previously permitted were withheld. Commentators note the structure, since the restriction is presented as a response rather than as an arbitrary burden. What was withheld is described only as good things, without a list, and the Quran supplies more detail on this elsewhere.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the section addressed to communities holding earlier scripture. Commentators connect the restriction to dietary limits described in earlier revelation, and discuss which of them are meant. The passage forms part of a longer list of consequences, each attached to a named conduct, which is how the classical commentaries read its structure.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for what is pure and pleasant, used across the Quran of permitted food. Its use makes the restriction a loss of something good rather than the removal of something harmful.
A verbal noun covering both turning aside oneself and blocking others. The construction attaches the consequence to obstruction of other people rather than only to their own conduct.
An adjective of quantity closing the clause. Commentators read it as attaching either to the number of people turned away or to the frequency of the turning, and they record both.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food restrictions were among the most visible markers distinguishing communities in the region, more visible than belief itself. What a household would and would not eat determined who could share a meal with whom, and shared meals were how alliances and marriages were built. A restriction on good food therefore reached deep into daily social life.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere states that restrictions of this kind were imposed as a consequence rather than belonging to the original guidance, and describes a later message as lifting some of them. The idea that a limit can be a response to conduct rather than a permanent feature runs through several passages.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Presenting a restriction as a consequence changes what it is. It is neither arbitrary nor intrinsic but responsive, which means the moral history of a community is described as shaping what remains available to it. The passage also attaches weight to obstructing others, treating the effect on other people's access as a matter separate from one's own conduct.

crossReferences.why: Names specific restrictions and says they were a recompense for wrongdoing committed.
States that food was lawful before, apart from what one community restricted for itself.
Describes a messenger who lifts burdens and removes the shackles that were upon them.

studies.applyIt: Think about a restriction in your own life that arrived as a consequence: a limit on your time, your money, your freedom, brought about by something you did. Rather than resenting it, name the conduct it followed from. That naming is the whole of what this passage does, and it usually changes the resentment.

studies.title: Taking What Was Closed Off
studies.meaning: Two financial charges close the list, and they are related. Taking increase on a loan when it had been closed off to them, and consuming people's wealth without any real basis. Commentators note that the two are named together because the second explains the first: what makes the increase an offence in this account is that it takes from someone with nothing underneath it. The clause about punishment then narrows to the faithless among them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the list of consequences addressed to communities holding earlier scripture. Commentators note that the community in Medina was itself receiving instruction on lending during the same period, so the charge is made in a setting where the subject was live for everyone. The final clause limits the statement rather than extending it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to grow or to swell. The word names the increase itself rather than the transaction, so the Quran describes the thing that expands rather than the arrangement producing it.
From a root meaning to be void or come to nothing. The same phrase appeared earlier in this surah, of wealth taken between believers with no real basis under it.
A partitive phrase, meaning some of them rather than all. Its placement before the punishment restricts the statement, which the commentators consistently note when reading the passage.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Lending in that economy was often between neighbours and against a harvest that had not yet come in. A loan that grew while a debtor's crop failed could take a grove that had been in a family for generations. Everyone had watched it happen, which is why the practice is treated across the Quran as a matter of what happens to people.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for increase on a loan comes from a root meaning growth, and the same root gives Arabic its ordinary words for raising a child and for a hill. The language names the practice by what it does, which is to swell, rather than by any judgement attached to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing the two charges together defines the first by the second. What is objected to is not increase as such but wealth moving from one person to another with nothing real underneath the movement. That grounds the matter in a relationship rather than in a mechanism, and the closing partitive keeps the statement from becoming a description of everyone.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about consuming wealth without ground, there addressed to believers.
Addresses the same practice at length, and describes what a lender is left with.
Contrasts what is given to increase through people's wealth with what is given seeking God.

studies.applyIt: Look at your income and identify anything that arrives without a corresponding thing having been done or given. Not in order to condemn it, simply to see it clearly. The standard in this passage is whether something real sits under a transfer of wealth, and that question is worth asking of your own arrangements.

studies.title: Firmly Rooted In Knowledge
studies.meaning: After a long list of failures, the passage turns and names an exception with unusual warmth. Those firmly rooted in knowledge among them, and the believers, are described as accepting what was revealed to this Prophet and what came before him. Then four practices are listed and a great reward promised. Commentators note that the exception is not grudging: it is fuller and more specific than the accusation preceding it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the address to communities holding earlier scripture. Commentators report that individuals from those communities had accepted the message, and read this ayah as naming them. The reports differ on identification while agreeing that the exception describes actual people rather than a theoretical category, which shapes how the passage is read.

keyTerms.note: A participle from a verb used of mountains set firmly into the earth. Knowledge is described as depth of footing rather than as quantity, which is why the image is one of stability.
A participle from the verb to make something stand upright. Used of prayer it means keeping a practice standing rather than merely performing it whenever the occasion arises.
The ordinary word for a wage, with an adjective of magnitude. The phrase recurs through this surah, and its appearance here places this group inside the same promise given to believers.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scholarly communities in Medina held their learning in memory and in manuscript, transmitted through teachers across generations. A man described as deeply rooted in knowledge was a recognisable figure with standing inside his own community, and for such a person to accept a new message cost more than it would have cost anybody else.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for those firmly rooted in knowledge appears twice in the Quran, here and in a passage about the interpretation of ambiguous verses. In both places it names people whose depth of learning is connected with how they respond to something difficult rather than with how much they can recite.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exception is placed at the end of a list of failures and given more detail than the failures received, which changes the passage's weight. It also joins knowledge to acceptance rather than opposing them, describing depth of learning as what makes recognition possible. The four practices named are ordinary ones, so the exception rests on nothing exceptional.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for those firmly rooted in knowledge, facing verses that are ambiguous.
Names an upright group among the same communities, standing in prayer through the night.
Describes those whose eyes overflow when they recognise the truth in what was sent down.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you expect a person's learning to make them harder to reach rather than easier. This ayah connects depth of knowledge with the capacity to recognise something new. Ask one person who knows more than you about something what changed their mind most recently, and listen to the whole answer.

studies.title: As We Inspired Noah
studies.meaning: A single sentence establishes continuity by listing names. What comes to this Prophet is described in exactly the same terms as what came to Noah and those after him, and then a series of names follows, ending with a book given to David. Commentators note the order, which is not chronological throughout, and read the list as gathering rather than sequencing. The claim is made by juxtaposition rather than by argument.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, answering a demand for a written text and a series of disputes about which messengers to accept. Commentators read the list as the response to those disputes: rather than defending one claim, the passage sets it inside a series. The names chosen span several communities' traditions, which is part of how the argument works in that setting.

keyTerms.note: A verb for communicating something swiftly and privately, used of a signal or a gesture as well as of revelation. It names the manner rather than the content of what was given.
A plural word for the branches descending from a common ancestor. Its inclusion in a list of individuals widens the sentence from named prophets to whole lines of them.
From a root meaning to write or inscribe firmly. The Quran uses it of what was given to David, and the word names a written thing specifically inside a list of inspirations.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Genealogy was recited aloud and memorised, and a list of names was a recognised form of argument in Arabia rather than a decoration. To establish a claim, a speaker recited the line it belonged to. This ayah uses exactly that form, so its first hearers would have recognised the shape of the argument before weighing its content.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names twenty-five prophets in total, and several of the lists that gather them, including this one, place the names in an order that is not chronological. Commentators discuss the ordering in each case, generally reading it as thematic or rhythmic rather than as a claim about sequence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument is made structurally rather than by assertion. Placing a new claim inside a list of accepted ones asks the hearer to explain what would justify treating it differently, which shifts the burden. The passage also describes revelation as one continuous kind of event with many instances, which is the premise the preceding ayat depend on.

crossReferences.why: Gives a longer list of prophets, and states that they were guided and chosen.
Lists many of the same names and says we make no distinction between any of them.
Describes the selective belief this list is set against, accepting some and rejecting others.

studies.applyIt: Take something you find hard to accept and place it beside the things you already accept without difficulty. Ask honestly what makes the new one different, in specific terms. This ayah's whole method is that comparison, and the answer is often about familiarity rather than about evidence.

studies.title: Messengers Not Told To You
studies.meaning: The list of names is closed with a statement that changes its scope: there were also messengers whose accounts were never given. So the list was never a census. Then one figure is singled out by the manner of address rather than by rank, with the verb for speaking repeated as its own noun, an Arabic intensive. The second ayah gives the purpose of sending them at all, which is stated as the removal of an argument.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage that answered demands about which messengers to accept. Commentators read the admission of untold accounts as answering a specific move in that argument, since a community could otherwise measure a new claim against a fixed and known list. The passage then generalises from named individuals to the purpose of prophecy itself.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to follow a track, which also gives the word for a story. A narrative in Arabic is pictured as following footprints rather than as composing something.
A verbal noun repeating the verb before it, an Arabic construction used for emphasis. It rules out any reading in which the speaking would be figurative rather than real.
A word for a proof advanced in dispute, from a root about aiming for something. The purpose of sending messengers is stated as removing a case people could otherwise make.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A claim in Arabia was tested against what people already knew, and a genealogy or a list of names was how such knowledge was held. Saying that the list is incomplete removed the ability to check a claim by looking it up in memory, which was the standard method available in a society without archives.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names twenty-five prophets and states here that others were sent whose accounts were not given. Commentators have generally declined to speculate about numbers, and the tradition's usual answer to the question of how many there were is that only God knows.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The purpose of prophecy is given as the removal of an excuse, which is a striking way to state it. Messengers are described as closing off a case people could otherwise bring, so revelation is framed as a matter of fairness in judgement rather than only as guidance. And the incompleteness of the list keeps any community from claiming the whole record.

crossReferences.why: States again that messengers were sent whose accounts were not related to you.
Says God does not punish until a messenger has been sent, the same principle stated directly.
Narrates the occasion of speaking with Moses, and what was asked and answered there.

studies.applyIt: Notice how confidently you dismiss things that fall outside the account you were given. This ayah tells its first audience that their record was incomplete by design. Hold one such gap open this week rather than filling it, and see whether anything you were certain of loosens slightly.

studies.title: The Angels Bear Witness
studies.meaning: Testimony is offered where agreement has not been reached. God is described as bearing witness to what was sent down, and a clause is added about the manner of sending: it was sent with His knowledge. Then a second witness is named, the angels, and the sentence closes by saying God suffices as a witness. Commentators note that a witness is not an argument, which is why the ayah opens with a word for contrast.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the section addressed to communities holding earlier scripture, after a long exchange of claims. Commentators read the opening particle as marking a turn: the argument is not continued but set aside in favour of testimony. The passage arrives at a point where the disagreement had been stated fully on both sides.

keyTerms.note: From the root for presence. A witness testifies to what he was there for, so the verb makes the claim rest on presence at the event rather than on reasoning about it.
A phrase commentators read in more than one way: that it was sent containing His knowledge, or sent by it. Both readings are recorded, and the grammar sustains each of them.
A verb meaning to be enough, used across this surah in closing clauses. Its effect is to end an argument by declaring that nothing further needs to be added to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Witnesses were the foundation of every claim in that society, and their number and standing decided outcomes. A dispute that could not be settled by argument was settled by who would stand and testify. Ending a long disagreement by naming witnesses used the exact procedure people expected, applied at a scale they could not contest.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying that God suffices as a witness appears several times across the Quran, always at the close of a passage rather than at its opening. Commentators note the placement: it functions as a seal on an argument already made rather than as a premise offered at the start of one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Shifting from argument to testimony changes what is being asked of the hearer. An argument invites a counter-argument; a witness invites either acceptance or the charge that the witness is unreliable. Naming the angels alongside makes the testimony plural, and the closing clause then declares the first witness sufficient on its own.

crossReferences.why: Answers a denial of messengership by naming God as sufficient witness between the parties.
Asks what thing is greatest in testimony, and answers that God is witness between us.
States that God is sufficient as a witness, earlier in this same surah.

studies.applyIt: Notice how long you keep arguing after the point where nothing new is being said. Both sides have usually stated everything by then. Try ending one such exchange this week by simply saying what you believe and stopping, without requiring the other person to concede anything.

studies.title: Except The Road To Hell
studies.meaning: Three short ayat that narrow as they go. The first names refusal together with turning others away, and calls the result a straying that has gone far. The second adds wrongdoing and states that neither forgiveness nor guidance to a road will come. The third then supplies the one road that remains, which is a grim piece of wordplay: guidance is withheld, and a route is named anyway.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the long argument with those who had refused the message while working to turn others from it. Commentators note that the passage names two things together throughout, refusal and obstruction, and read the pairing as the reason for its severity. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: A verb covering both turning aside oneself and obstructing others. Its presence alongside refusal is what distinguishes the people described from those who simply did not accept.
A different word from the one used for a path elsewhere in this surah, and it recurs in the next ayah. The repetition is what makes the third ayah land as it does.
An adjective for what costs no effort. Closing a severe passage with it removes any suggestion of struggle, which is the same move made earlier in this surah about the Fire.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Roads in that landscape were few and known by name, and a traveller who lost one had no alternative to find. Being told there was no road was a complete statement about a journey. Naming a road and then specifying which one carried the same weight as a guide pointing at the only track and saying where it ended.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a road appears in two consecutive ayat here, first as what is withheld and then as what is nonetheless supplied. Arabic wordplay of this kind, repeating a term to reverse its force, appears throughout the Quran, and commentators regularly point it out in passages of warning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is careful to name two things rather than one. Refusal alone is described elsewhere in the Quran with much wider openings left; here obstruction of others is added, and the severity follows that addition. That places particular weight on the effect a person has on other people's access, treating it as a separate matter from their own position.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for a straying that has gone far, earlier in this surah.
Adds punishment upon punishment for those who refused and turned others from God's path.
Names those who refused and obstructed and then died refusing, and what follows for them.

studies.applyIt: Consider the difference these ayat draw. It is one thing to hold back from something yourself, and another to make it harder for the people around you. Ask whether anyone finds a good thing harder because of how you speak about it, and adjust that one thing this week.

studies.title: Better For You
studies.meaning: The address widens for the first time in a long stretch, moving from particular communities to people in general. The Messenger has come with the truth, and belief is recommended in two words that function as an assessment rather than a command: better for you. The alternative is then met with the statement of ownership used throughout the surah's closing sections, so refusal changes nothing about what is held.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's long argument and turning outward. Commentators note the shift in address, from those given earlier scripture to humanity, and read the ayah as the summary the whole section has been building toward. The statement about the heavens and the earth recurs here as it does several times in these later passages.

keyTerms.note: The widest form of address in the Quran, used of humanity rather than of believers or of a named community. Its appearance here marks the end of a long stretch of particular argument.
A word covering truth, reality and a rightful claim together. Saying he came with it rather than about it makes the truth something carried rather than something asserted.
A comparative with the beneficiary named. It states an assessment rather than an instruction, which is why the sentence reads as advice offered rather than as a demand made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca and Medina sat on routes that carried people from Yemen, Syria, Abyssinia and Persia, and the population of a market town on such a route was genuinely mixed. An address to people in general was not rhetorical in that setting. A speaker in a market could reasonably expect several communities to be within hearing.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah is the first in the Quran's arrangement to open with an address to humanity rather than to believers, and it returns to that address here near its close. Commentators note the framing, since the chapter's opening and its final section both widen the audience in the same way.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting the appeal as an assessment rather than a command changes the relationship it assumes. The hearer is treated as someone weighing a benefit, not as someone under an order, which fits an address to people who have not accepted any authority yet. And the clause about ownership makes clear that the benefit named runs entirely in one direction.

crossReferences.why: Opens the surah with the same wide address to humanity, before any particular community.
Repeats the address a few ayat later, naming a proof and a clear light instead.
Says whoever is guided is guided for himself, and whoever strays does so against himself.

studies.applyIt: Notice how differently you receive advice framed as a command and the same advice framed as an assessment of your own benefit. Try giving one piece of advice this week in the second form, and watch how much of the resistance you usually meet was caused by the framing.

studies.title: Do Not Go To Excess
studies.meaning: An address is made to those holding earlier scripture, and the instruction is against excess in religion rather than against religion. Jesus is then described with three titles the Quran affirms: a messenger of God, His word delivered to Mary, and a spirit from Him. What follows is a statement of oneness and a closing declaration that God is far above having a son. Christians read these matters differently, which is what the passage is addressing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, near the surah's close. Commentators place the passage among exchanges with Christian communities of the region, and some connect it to a delegation that came to discuss such questions. The reports differ on which occasion is meant. What the classical commentaries agree on is that the ayah addresses claims about Jesus rather than his standing as a prophet.

keyTerms.note: A verb for exceeding a proper limit, used of a price rising too high. The fault named is excess rather than devotion, so the instruction is about measure rather than about direction.
A title the Quran affirms of Jesus. Commentators read it in connection with the word of command by which he was created, and record the discussion rather than reducing it to one sense.
A phrase the commentators handle carefully, generally reading the preposition as marking origin rather than part. The Quran uses the same construction elsewhere of things granted by God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Christian communities in Najran, Syria and Abyssinia were substantial, and their doctrinal debates were themselves live and unresolved across the region in that century. Traders and travellers carried those debates into Arabian markets. Questions about how Jesus should be described were therefore familiar to the Quran's first audience rather than remote.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran affirms three titles for Jesus inside this ayah while disputing another claim, so the passage is affirming and denying in a single sentence. Commentators note that it also opens by addressing its audience with a respectful form, naming them by their scripture rather than by their disagreement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction is against excess rather than against reverence, which locates the disagreement precisely. Titles are affirmed, and then a limit is drawn on what may be said about God. The passage also grounds that limit in ownership: everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, so nothing needs to be attributed to Him in the way of family.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same instruction against excess in religion, addressed in almost identical terms.
States the same conclusion after the account of Jesus, that God takes no son.
Compares the creation of Jesus with that of Adam, both by a word of command.

studies.applyIt: Notice where your admiration for someone has quietly outgrown what you would say about them in plain words. It happens with teachers, parents, leaders and writers. The instruction here concerns measure rather than affection, and saying the plain version once usually restores the measure without costing the affection.

studies.title: Never Too Proud To Serve
studies.meaning: A single verb carries the ayah, meaning to hold oneself above something out of pride. The Messiah is described as never doing that with respect to servanthood, and the angels brought near are named alongside him. The argument works upward: if those closest do not consider service beneath them, the question of who might is answered by implication. The closing clause then gathers everyone regardless.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the passage that addressed excess in describing Jesus. Commentators read the two together, since this ayah answers the same question from another direction: rather than disputing a title, it describes what the figure in question is reported as accepting. The angels are added because they were also the subject of claims in the region.

keyTerms.note: A rare verb built from a root about turning the face aside. It names refusal out of pride specifically, rather than refusal for any other reason, which is what the ayah is measuring.
The ordinary word for one who serves, used across the Quran of prophets in their highest moments. Its use here makes servanthood a description of nearness rather than of lowliness.
A passive participle from the verb to bring close. The nearness is described as granted rather than achieved, which is why the word can sit beside a statement about not disdaining service.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Service in Arabia was a matter of standing, and a free man guarded the distinction carefully. To be called someone's servant was an insult unless the master was extraordinary, in which case it became a boast. That is the register the ayah works in: attachment to a great house was a claim to honour, not a confession of low rank.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran refers to its own Prophet as a servant of God at the most exalted moments described in the book, including the night journey and the sending down of revelation. The title is reserved for those points rather than for ordinary ones, which is the pattern this ayah relies on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a claim about status by describing what status looks like from inside. Those nearest are the ones least inclined to hold service beneath them, which inverts the usual relationship between rank and deference. That makes pride a mark of distance rather than of height, and it grounds the argument in disposition rather than in doctrine.

crossReferences.why: States that everyone in the heavens and earth comes to the Merciful only as a servant.
Describes the angels as honoured servants who do not speak ahead of Him.
Names the Prophet as a servant at the very moment of the night journey.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the tasks you consider beneath you: the cleaning, the setting up, the message you think somebody junior should send. Do one of them this week without arranging for anyone to notice. The ayah's argument is that distance from that reluctance is what nearness actually looks like.

studies.title: Paid In Full, And More
studies.meaning: Two outcomes are given in one sentence, and the asymmetry is deliberate. The first group is paid its wages in full and then increased from God's bounty, so the account is settled and then exceeded. The second, described by the pride named in the ayah before, is met with punishment and with the absence of any protector or helper. The two halves are built in matching grammar so the difference is audible.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about servanthood and pride that began with the Messiah and the angels. Commentators read the ayah as the outcome attached to the disposition just described, so the subject remains the same across the three ayat. The surah is in its final section, gathering its arguments toward a close.

keyTerms.gloss: He will pay them in full
keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for completing a payment without shortfall. It belongs to the vocabulary of settling a debt, which is why the increase mentioned next is described separately from it.
The ordinary verb for adding more. Its placement after full payment is what makes the sentence generous, since nothing further was owed once the account had been settled.
A verb meaning to make oneself great, from the root for bigness. Paired with the rare verb of the previous ayah, it names the disposition rather than any particular act.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A day labourer in Medina was paid at the end of the work, and whether he was paid in full and on time was a matter people spoke about. A master who added something beyond the agreed wage was remembered for it. The ayah's two verbs describe exactly that sequence, which its first hearers would have recognised at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage names the reward in two stages, full payment and then increase, a structure that recurs across the Quran wherever wages are described. Commentators note that the second stage is always attributed to bounty rather than to the accounting, so it is never described as owed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Separating payment from increase preserves both justice and generosity without letting either absorb the other. What was earned is settled exactly; what is added comes from a different source entirely. The other half of the sentence then names the absence of a protector, which returns to a phrase used across this surah for the position of someone standing entirely alone.

crossReferences.why: Names the disposition whose two outcomes this ayah sets out in matching construction.
Uses the same pairing, full payment of wages followed by an increase from His bounty.
States earlier in this surah that no protector or helper is found besides God.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time somebody gave you more than was agreed, and how differently that landed from being paid exactly what was owed. Do that once this week for a person who works for you or with you. The distinction this ayah draws is small in size and large in effect.

studies.title: A Proof And A Light
studies.meaning: The wide address returns and two things are named as having arrived: a proof from your Lord, and a clear light sent down. The commentators discuss what each refers to and generally read them together, one term drawn from argument and one from perception. The second ayah then describes what follows for those who believe and take hold, ending on a straight path leading to Him rather than merely to a destination.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's closing section. Commentators note that the address to humanity appears twice within a few ayat here, framing the end of the chapter as it framed its opening. The passage arrives after a long argument, and it summarises by naming what has been given rather than by restating any of the disputes.

keyTerms.note: A word for decisive evidence, from a root connected with brightness. Arabic ties proof to light at the level of the root, which is why the two terms in this ayah sit together naturally.
Light paired with an adjective meaning both clear in itself and clarifying. The doubling makes the light not only visible but the means by which other things become visible too.
From a root meaning to grasp something for protection, used of clinging to a rope. It names an action rather than a state, which is why it stands beside believing rather than inside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel at night in open country was done by starlight, and a lamp carried through a settlement marked where a person was going and who was moving at that hour. Light was scarce and therefore practical rather than decorative. Describing something as a clear light named it as the difference between moving and waiting.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for a decisive proof comes from a root associated with brightness and shining. The language ties evidence to light at the level of the root, so the two nouns in this ayah are closer to one another in Arabic than the English words proof and light suggest.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Pairing a proof with a light distinguishes two things that are often confused: something that settles an argument, and something that lets you see. The second ayah then adds a third element, taking hold, so belief is described as needing a grip and not only an assent. The path named at the close leads to God rather than to a place.

crossReferences.why: Describes a light and a clear Book as having come from God to the same audience.
Uses the same verb for holding fast, there of holding to the rope of God together.
Opens the same wide address a few ayat earlier, naming truth rather than light.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between being convinced of something and being able to see by it. Most people have beliefs of the first kind and very few of the second. Take one thing you are convinced of and use it this week to decide something, which is the only way the second kind is ever formed.

studies.title: The Case Left Open
studies.meaning: The surah closes by answering the one inheritance case it had left unfinished, an estate with neither parent nor child, and by naming the siblings' shares in it. Then a short clause gives the reason for the whole passage: God makes this clear so that you do not go astray. Commentators note that the surah's last word before the closing name concerns straying, which is the same word it has used throughout.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and reported as among the last passages of the surah to be revealed. Commentators transmit that a question about this case was raised repeatedly and answered here, and several accounts describe it as the response to an illness during which a man asked how his estate would be divided. The reports differ in detail while agreeing on the substance.

keyTerms.gloss: an estate with no direct heirs
keyTerms.note: The rare term left partly open earlier in this surah. Commentators discuss its exact scope at length and record the difficulty, generally reading it as an estate with neither parent nor child.
A verb for coming to an end, used of a person dying and of things being destroyed. Its plainness is notable in a passage otherwise built from precise legal vocabulary.
The verb for losing one's road, used repeatedly across this surah. Its appearance in the reason given for the passage ties inheritance to the same image used of belief.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man with no children and no surviving parents left an estate that families genuinely fought over, since custom offered no settled answer and everyone with a claim had a case. Such disputes could last years and split households permanently. That is why a question about this particular case was asked repeatedly rather than once.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah closes the surah by returning to the subject its opening ayat began with, so the chapter ends where it started, on the property of those left behind. The unfinished case named earlier in the surah is completed only in its final ayah, which is an unusually deliberate piece of construction.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reason given for the detail is that people should not go astray, using the same word this surah applies to belief and to conduct. That connects precision about shares to the moral life directly: without a clear division, families lose their way in a manner the passage treats as continuous with any other kind of straying. Clarity is presented as a mercy rather than as a constraint.

crossReferences.why: Raises this same case earlier in the surah and leaves part of it unresolved there.
Sets out the shares for children and parents that this ayah completes for siblings.
States the principle these shares implement, that men and women both hold a fixed portion.

studies.applyIt: If you have never written down what should happen to what you leave, do the first small piece of it this week: a list, a note, a conversation with one person. The reason given here is that clarity keeps people from losing their way, and the losing usually happens between people who loved each other.
